children.text: ataḥ paraṃ cāturvarṇyasādhāraṇadharmasaṅkṣepakathanād uttarasmin kāle sa eva vistarakathanasyocito 'vasaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, after this, since a brief statement has been made of the dharmas common to the four varṇas, in the following section this is indeed the proper occasion for stating them at length.

children.text: bahugranthapāṭhe śaktirahitān mandaprajñān prati saṅkṣepeṇābhihite sati samarthānām uttamaprajñānāṃ buddhisthatvāt tān prati vistareṇa kathayitum ucitatvāt ||
children.translated_text: For when they have been stated briefly for people of weak capacity and dull understanding, who lack the power to study extensive texts, they are present in the minds of capable people of excellent understanding; therefore it is appropriate to state them at length for them.
For this very reason the teachers say:
For by both brevity and fullness, for men of dull and excellent intellect alike,
the matter being spoken enters the inner faculty; therefore it is described.
So it is said.
Or else, 'after this' means after the statement of dharma whose chief fruit is in the next world.

children.text: ṣaṭkarmābhirataḥ sandhyāsnānam ityādinā hyāmuṣmikaphale dharme 'bhihite sati aihikaphalasya kṛṣyādidharmasya buddhisthatvāt tadabhidhānasya yadukto 'vasaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: For, when dharma bearing fruit in the next world has been stated by the words beginning 'devoted to the six duties, twilight worship and bathing,' then, since the dharma such as agriculture whose fruit is worldly is present to the mind, the occasion for stating it is the one mentioned.

children.text: vakṣyamāṇasya kṛṣyādidharmasya brahmacārivanasthayatiṣv asambhavam abhipretya tadyogyam āśramiṇaṃ darśayati gṛhasthasya iti kṛtatretādvāpareṣu vaiśyasyaiva kṛṣyādāvadhikāro na tu gṛhasthamātrasya viprādeḥ ato viśinaṣṭi kalau yuge iti ||
children.translated_text: With regard to the forthcoming dharma of agriculture and the like, considering its impossibility among students, forest-dwellers, and renunciants, he indicates the āśramin to whom it is suited by the word 'of the householder.' In the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages only the Vaiśya has authority over agriculture and the like, not every householder such as a Brahmin; therefore he specifies, 'in the Kali age.'
The word <s>karma</s> is used in ordinary speech merely for activity.

children.text: ācāraśabdaśca dharmarūpe śāstrīye vyāpāre kṛṣyādestu yugāntareṣu karmatvam ||
children.translated_text: And the word <s>ācāra</s> is used for scriptural activity having the form of dharma; but agriculture and the like have the status of <s>karma</s> in the other ages.
In the Kali age they have the status of <s>ācāra</s>; thus they possess both forms.
Likewise, in the other āśramas they have the status of <s>karma</s>, while for householdership they have the stated status of <s>ācāra</s>; thus there is a double form.
With that intention he said 'karmācāra,' action and conduct.

children.text: kalau gṛhasthasya yājanādīnāṃ durlabhatvājjīvanahetutayā kṛṣyādividhānād ācāratvam upapannam ||
children.translated_text: Since in the Kali age sacrificial officiating and the like are difficult for a householder to obtain, the prescription of agriculture and the like as a means of livelihood is reasonably <s>ācāra</s>.
He establishes that agriculture and the like are a common dharma by saying 'belonging to the four varṇas and the āśrama.'
The four varṇas themselves are called <s>cāturvarṇya</s>.
And that is well known everywhere.
The āśrama is the one having the form of householdership.
For Śūdras too have householders' dharmas such as marriage and the five great sacrifices.
All this will be explained very clearly by us later, in the examination of the āśramas.
Because it is prescribed in that āśrama, it is common.
By the word <s>Parāśara</s> here is intended the one who arose in a past kalpa.
To make precisely this clear, the word 'formerly' was used.

children.text: pūrvakalpasiddhaṃ parāśaravākyaṃ kalidharme kṛṣyādau yathāvṛttaṃ tathaivāhaṃ sampravakṣyāmi ||
children.translated_text: I shall declare exactly as it occurred the statement of <s>Parāśara</s>, established in a former kalpa, concerning Kali-age dharma such as agriculture.

children.text: ataḥ sampradāyāgatatvāt kṛṣyāder ācāratāyāṃ na vivādaḥ kartavya ityāśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The intention is that, because agriculture and the like have come down through tradition, no dispute should be raised about their status as <s>ācāra</s>.

children.text: gurutaraviṣaye vinayaḥ kartavyaḥ iti śiṣṭācāraṃ śikṣayituṃ śaktyā sampravakṣyāmi ityuktam ||
children.translated_text: In order to teach the conduct of the learned, namely that humility should be shown concerning weighty matters, he said, 'I shall declare it according to my ability.'

children.text: na tu kasmiṃścid dharme svasya aśaktiṃ dyotayitum ||
children.translated_text: He did not say this to indicate his own incapacity with regard to any dharma.
For incapacity in that matter is impossible for <s>Parāśara</s>, who is expert in the dharma of the Kali age.
He shows the dharma that has been promised.
The six duties are the previously mentioned ones, beginning with sacrificing and officiating, and also those beginning with twilight worship.

children.text: taiḥ sahito vipraḥ śuśrūṣakaiḥ śūdraiḥ kṛṣiṃ kārayet ||
children.translated_text: A Brahmin, furnished with them, should have agriculture performed by Śūdras who serve him.

children.text: na ca yājanādīnāṃ jīvanahetutvāt kim anayā kṛṣyā iti vācyam ||
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said, 'Since officiating at sacrifices and the like are means of livelihood, what need is there of this agriculture?'
For in the Kali age officiating and the like are difficult to obtain in a measure sufficient for livelihood.
But as for what was said by <s>Manu</s>:
'Even while living by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, a Brahmin or even a Kṣatriya
should carefully avoid agriculture, which is mostly injurious and dependent on others.'

children.text: kṛṣiṃ sādhviti manyante sā vṛttiḥ sadvigarhitā
children.translated_text: 'They think agriculture good, but that occupation is censured by the good;
the wooden implement with iron point kills the earth and the beings lying in the earth.'
So it is said.
That has reference to agriculture done by oneself.
Otherwise there would be contradiction with <s>Manu</s>'s own statement.
For agriculture has been accepted by that very author:
'If, not living by either of the two, the question should arise, How could he subsist?',
'then he should live by resorting to agriculture and cattle-tending, the livelihood of a Vaiśya.'
So it is said.
Objection: in the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>, agriculture done by oneself is accepted:

children.text: svayaṃ vā karṣaṇaṃ kuryādvāṇijyaṃ vā kusīdakam
children.translated_text: 'He may himself do ploughing, or trade, or money-lending;'
'money-lending is a hard and very sinful occupation; therefore he should avoid it.'
So it is said.
That is not so.
For this statement is chiefly a censure of money-lending.
For this very reason <s>Nārada</s> says:

children.text: āpatsv api ca kaṣṭāsu brāhmaṇasya na vārddhuṣam ||
children.translated_text: 'Even in severe calamities, lending at interest is not for a Brahmin.'
So it is said.
Objection: <s>Bṛhaspati</s> accepted agriculture performed by oneself:
'He may undertake money-lending, agriculture, and trade not done by himself;'
'in a time of distress, if a twice-born man does it himself, he is not joined with sin.'
So it is said.
Granted.
But doing it oneself applies to one who is unable even to have it done by others.
For it is qualified by the phrase 'in a time of distress.'
Objection: even having it done by others concerns only distress.
For agriculture is the dharma of a Vaiśya, while for a Brahmin the principal means of livelihood are officiating at sacrifices and the like.
If so, then let the rule be arranged according to degrees of distress.
In a slight distress there is having it done by others; in an extreme distress there is doing it oneself.
Or else, let it be arranged according to the difference of age.
In other ages, having it done by others is an emergency dharma; in the Kali age it is the principal dharma.
Because it is introduced and taught as the principal topic.

children.text: tatra kṛṣau halasya ekasya balīvardasaṃkhyāniyamam āha hārītaḥ
children.translated_text: There, regarding agriculture, <s>Hārīta</s> states the rule about the number of oxen for one plough:
A righteous plough has eight oxen; for those seeking mere livelihood, six oxen.
For cruel men it has four oxen; for killers of Brahmins, two oxen.
Thus.

children.text: tatrāntyau pakṣau heyau itarāvapi krameṇa mukhyānukalpau draṣṭavyau ||
children.translated_text: In this matter the last two alternatives are to be rejected; the other two also should be understood respectively as the principal rule and the substitute rule.
He states which oxen are to be avoided in agriculture.
Thus.
Hunger and the rest are to be understood from their respective signs.
'Deficient in limb' means crippled in the feet.
'Impotent' means devoid of maleness.

children.text: kīdṛśastarhi balīvardaḥ kṛṣau yojya ityata āha ||
children.translated_text: Then what sort of ox should be yoked in agriculture? In answer to this he says:
Thus.
'Firm-limbed' means free from defects of the feet and so on.
'Free from disease' means not afflicted by illness.
'Satisfied' means not distressed by hunger and thirst.

children.text: sunardo hisako dṛptaḥ śramarahitaḥ iti yāvat ||
children.translated_text: 'Well-bellowing, vigorous, proud' means, in short, free from fatigue.
In the phrase 'not gelded,' the expression is governed chiefly by the abstract condition.
It means free from gelding, endowed with maleness, and capable.
Half of the day means two watches.

children.text: paścāt snānaṃ samācaret iti balīvardān snāpayedityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Afterwards he should perform bathing' means that he should bathe the oxen.
And accordingly <s>Hārīta</s> says:
Having bathed and adorned the oxen, he should feed Brahmins.
Thus.
A special rule concerning hauling is shown in the <s>Āśvamedhika</s>:
He should make them draw only by a call of 'huṃ,' or by a leafy branch.

children.text: na daṇḍena na yaṣṭyā vā na pāśena ca vā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Not with a rod, nor with a staff, nor again with a noose.
He should not make one draw when wearied by hunger, thirst, and toil, or when its senses are impaired.

children.text: sutṛpteṣu ca bhuñjīyāt pibet pīteṣu codakam ||
children.translated_text: When they are well satisfied he may eat, and when they have drunk he may drink water.

children.text: ahnaḥ pūrvaṃ dviyāmaṃ vā dhuryāṇāṃ vāhanaṃ smṛtam
children.translated_text: The hauling of draught animals is prescribed for the first two watches of the day.
In the middle part and in the last part he should let them rest as they please.

children.text: yatra vā tvarayā kṛtyaṃ saṃśayo yatra cādhvani
children.translated_text: Where there is urgent work, or where there is danger on the road,

children.text: vāhayet tatra dhuryāṃstu na sa pāpena lipyate ||
children.translated_text: there he may make the draught animals draw, and he is not stained by sin.

children.text: anyathā vāhayan rājan niyataṃ yāti rauravam
children.translated_text: But making them draw otherwise, O king, he certainly goes to <s>Raurava</s>.
The lowest man who, from delusion, makes their blood flow,
incurs a sin equal to embryo-killing, O son of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>.
He states what is to be done after the bathing of the oxen.

children.text: yathā balīvardaśrāntikṛtadoṣāpanayanāya snāpanaṃ evaṃ prāṇyupaghātadoṣāpanayanāya yathāśakti japyādīnām anyatamam anutiṣṭhet ||
children.translated_text: Just as bathing removes the fault caused by the fatigue of the oxen, so, to remove the fault caused by injury to living beings, he should perform, according to his ability, one among recitation and the other rites.

children.text: ekaṃ dvau trīṃścaturo vā viprān snātakān yathāśakti bhojayet ||
children.translated_text: According to his ability, he should feed one, two, three, or four Brahmins who are snātakas.
The snātakas are the nine kinds of mendicants.
<s>Manu</s> states this:
One seeking offspring, one about to sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given all his wealth,
one seeking means for his teacher, for his father or mother, one seeking means for Vedic study, and one afflicted by illness.
Thus.
'One seeking offspring' means one seeking the goods needed for marriage for the sake of progeny.

children.text: sarvavedasaḥ sarvasvadakṣiṇaṃ yāgaṃ kṛtvā niḥsvatvam āpanno dravyārthī tam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'One who has given all his wealth' means one who, after performing a sacrifice with a fee consisting of all his possessions, has become destitute and seeks wealth; that is the sense.
'For father and mother' means one seeking means for service to father and mother.
'One seeking means for Vedic study' means one seeking wealth to maintain recitation and teaching of the Veda.
'Afflicted' means ill.

children.text: svādhyāyārthisahitaḥ upatāpī svādhyāyārthyupatāpī tamiti madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Afflicted along with one seeking means for Vedic study' means 'one seeking means for Vedic study and one afflicted'; this is a compound with the middle member elided.
The meaning is 'both of those two.'
He states the use of grain produced in agriculture.
Thus.

children.text: yāni svayaṃkṛṣṭe kṣetre phalitāni dhānyāni yāni dāsaiḥ karṣite kṣetre svayam arjitāni dhānyāni taiḥ sarvaiḥ smārttān pañcamahāyajñān śrautīm agniṣṭomādikratudīkṣāṃ ca kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: With all the grains that have borne fruit in a field ploughed by oneself, and with the grains acquired by oneself from a field ploughed by servants, one should perform the five smārta great sacrifices and also the śrauta consecration for rites such as the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>.
'He should cause to perform' contains the causative suffix ṇic used in the sense of one's own action.
Or else he himself should perform the great sacrifices.

children.text: yiyakṣubhyo dhānyaṃ dattvā taiḥ kratudīkṣāṃ ca kārayet ||
children.translated_text: Having given grain to those who wish to sacrifice, he should cause them to undertake consecration for a rite.
In the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s> too this use is shown:
Having obtained gain, he should honor the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins.

children.text: te tṛptāstasya taddoṣaṃ śamayanti na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When satisfied, they pacify that fault of his; there is no doubt.
Thus.

children.text: kṛṣīvalasya tilādidhānyasampannasya dhanalobhena prasaktas tilādivikrayastaṃ nivārayati ||
children.translated_text: For a farmer who possesses sesame and other grains, he forbids the sale of sesame and the like, undertaken through greed for wealth.
Thus.
'Flavors' means curds, honey, ghee, and so on.

children.text: yadi dhānyāntararahitasya tilavikrayamantareṇa jīvanaṃ vā dharmo vā na sidhyet tadā tilā dhānyāntarair vinimātavyāḥ ityabhipretya vikreyā dhānyatatsamāḥ ityuktam ||
children.translated_text: If for one who lacks other grain neither life nor <s>dharma</s> could be maintained without selling sesame, then sesame should be exchanged for other grains; with this intention it is said that they may be sold for grain equal to them.

children.text: yāvadbhiḥ prasthaistilā dattāstāvadbhir eva dhānyāntaramupādeyaṃ nādhikamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that as many prasthas of sesame as are given, exactly that much other grain is to be accepted, not more.
That has been stated by <s>Nārada</s>:
In incapacity, for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the sake of sacrifice,
if sesame must necessarily be sold, it should be sold for an equal amount of grain.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> also says:
For the sake of <s>dharma</s>, sesame may be brought to sale for an equal amount of grain.
Thus.
The rule concerning sesame should also be applied to flavors.
For this very reason <s>Manu</s> says:

children.text: rasā rasairnimātavyā na tveva lavaṇaṃ rasaiḥ
children.translated_text: Flavors are to be exchanged for flavors, but salt certainly not for flavors.
Cooked food is to be exchanged for uncooked food, and sesame for an equal amount of grain.
Thus.
<s>Āpastamba</s> also says:

children.text: annena cānnasya manuṣyāṇāṃ ca manuṣyaiḥ rasānāṃ ca rasaiḥ gandhānāṃ ca gandhairvidyayā ca vidyānām ||
children.translated_text: Food is to be exchanged with food, humans with humans, flavors with flavors, perfumes with perfumes, and forms of knowledge with knowledge.
Thus.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> states a special rule in the exchange of flavors:
Flavors may be exchanged for flavors, whether greater or lesser in quantity.
Thus.
<s>Gautama</s> states a special rule in the exchange of food:
For cooked food, however, exchange may be with an equal or unequal amount.
Thus.
Objection: the sale of sesame has been accepted by <s>Manu</s>:
Having willingly produced it in agriculture, the farmer himself
may sell pure sesame, for the sake of <s>dharma</s>, if it has not been kept long.
Thus.
Here some say that this is intended to indicate the absence of a fixed restriction.

children.text: apare tu manyante ṛṇāpākaraṇādyāvaśyakadharmārthe tilavikrayo na viruddhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, think that the sale of sesame is not opposed to rule when it is for an indispensable religious purpose, such as clearing a debt.
This latter view alone is reasonable.
Because it agrees with the statement of <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>:

children.text: kāmaṃ vā svayaṃ kṛṣyotpādya tilān vikrīṇīran ||
children.translated_text: Or, having themselves produced sesame by agriculture, they may sell it as they wish.
Thus.

children.text: vinimayābhiprāye tu vacanāntareṇa saha paunaruktyam aparihāryaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: But if the intention were exchange, then repetition with another statement would be unavoidable.

children.text: yato manunaiva vacanāntareṇa tilā dhānyena tatsamā iti niyamo darśitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For by another statement <s>Manu</s> himself has shown the rule that sesame is to be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
As for the fact that in another statement a prohibition on the sale of sesame seems to appear by implication,
for <s>Manu</s> and <s>Yama</s> have shown as follows:
Whatever else one does with sesame, apart from eating, anointing, and giving,
becoming a worm, he sinks together with his ancestors in dog excrement.
Thus.
This is not a fault.
Because its scope is what is other than an indispensable religious purpose.

children.text: yo 'yaṃ tilānāṃ dhānyasamatvena vinimayaḥ yaśca tṛṇādivikrayaṃ seyam evaṃvidhā viprasya jīvanārthā vṛttiḥ ||
children.translated_text: That exchange of sesame for grain on a basis of equality, and that sale of grass and the like, this sort of livelihood is for a Brahmin's subsistence.
And accordingly <s>Nārada</s> says:
For a Brahmin, dry wood, grass, and the like are saleable.
Thus.

children.text: idānīṃ kṛṣāvānuṣaṅgikasya pāpmanaḥ pratīkāraṃ vaktuṃ prathamatastaṃ pāpmānaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to state the remedy for the sin incidental to agriculture, he first shows that sin.
Thus.

children.text: kṛṣau hiṃsāyā avarjanīyatvāt sāvadhānasyāpi kṛṣīvalasya doṣo 'nuṣajyate iti ||
children.translated_text: Since injury is unavoidable in agriculture, fault attaches even to a careful farmer.
Here the statement of <s>Manu</s>, 'mostly involving injury,' has already been cited earlier.
He makes clear the greatness of the fault that has been stated.
Thus.

children.text: lohasahitena lāṅgalamukhena prāṇināṃ citravadho bhavatīti matsyavadhāt pāpādhikyamuktam ||
children.translated_text: Since varied slaughter of living beings occurs through the iron-tipped point of the plough, a greater sin than that from killing fish is stated.

children.text: uktarītyā karṣakamātrasya pāpaprasaktau tad vārayituṃ viśinaṣṭi ||
children.translated_text: When sin would, in the manner stated, apply to every farmer, he makes a qualification in order to ward that off.
Thus.
A pāśaka is one who spreads a net and catches deer and other animals.
A vyādha is one whose livelihood is the killing of deer.
A śākunika is one who kills birds.
The non-giver is one who does not give to those who have come to the threshing floor and the base of the grain heap.
The adverse consequence is the same for all of them.
Therefore the netter and the others are described here as examples.

children.text: yathā pāśakādīnāṃ pāpaṃ mahad evamevādātuḥ karṣakasyetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: just as the sin of the netter and the others is great, so too is that of the farmer who does not give.

children.text: yadarthaṃ kṛṣīvalasya pāpmā darśitaḥ tamidānīṃ pāpaparihāraprakāram āha ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the way to remove the sin for the sake of which the farmer's sin was shown.
Thus.

children.text: chedanabhedanahananair yāvanti pāpāni niṣpadyante teṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ khale dhānyadānaṃ pratīkāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: For all the sins that arise from cutting, splitting, and killing, the remedy is the gift of grain at the threshing floor.
And accordingly <s>Hārīta</s> says:
Having split the earth, cut plants, and killed insects and ants,
farmers are purified by the khalayajna; there is no doubt here.

children.text: yūpo 'yaṃ nihito madhye meḍhir nāma hi karṣakaiḥ
children.translated_text: This post set in the middle, called the meḍhi by farmers, is a sacrificial post.
Therefore, without neglect, one should give there the fee consisting of grain and wealth.
He states the adverse consequence when the khalayajna is not performed.
Thus.

children.text: karṣakasyāyaṃ khalayajño nityaḥ kāmyaśca iti vacanadvayabalād avagamyate ||
children.translated_text: On the strength of the two statements, it is understood that this khalayajna is both obligatory and optional for the farmer.

children.text: akaraṇe pratyavāyāt nityatvaṃ chedanādipāpanivartakatvāt kāmyatvaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: It is obligatory because there is adverse consequence if it is not performed, and it is optional because it removes the sin from cutting and the like.
The obligatory character of the khalayajna is shown in the <s>Śaivapurāṇa</s>:

children.text: adattvā karṣako devi yastu dhānyaṃ praveśayet
children.translated_text: O goddess, the farmer who brings in grain without having given any,
I shall tell the sin, O goddess, of that man overcome by greed.
For a thousand divine years that evil-minded cultivator
becomes a tree in a desert region, devoid of flowers and fruit.
At its end, having become human after some lapse of time,
he is born poor, sick, foolish, and of low family.
He states the measure of the grain that is to be given.
One part among six parts is a sixth part.
One part among parts numbered twenty-one is a twenty-first part.

children.text: tadvat triṃśakeṣu bhāgeṣvanyatamo bhāgastriṃśaḥ iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, among thirty parts, one part should be understood as a thirtieth part.
It should be given to the ancestors as well as to the gods.
That is stated in the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>:
One who practices agriculture should give a twentieth share to the gods and the ancestors,

children.text: triṃśadbhāgaṃ tu viprāṇāṃ kṛṣiṃ kurvanna doṣabhāk ||
children.translated_text: and a thirtieth share to the Brahmins; then he is not a sharer in fault.
Thus.
Having stated agriculture together with what is to be done by a Brahmin, he states it also for the other social classes.
Thus.

children.text: yadyapi vaiśyasya kṛṣiḥ pūrvādhyāye vihitā tathāpyatra itikartavyatāvidhānāya punarupanyāsaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although agriculture for the Vaiśya was prescribed in the previous chapter, it is mentioned again here in order to prescribe the procedure to be performed.

children.text: tathā kuryāt ityatideśena brāhmaṇasya kṛṣau vihitetikartavyatā sarvāpyatra vihitā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: By the extension expressed in 'he should do likewise,' all the procedure prescribed for the Brahmin's agriculture is prescribed here too.

children.text: kṛṣivat vāṇijyaśilpayorapi kalau varṇacatuṣṭayasādhāraṇyaṃ darśayituṃ vāṇijyaśilpakam ityuktam ||
children.translated_text: In order to show that, like agriculture, trade and crafts too are common to the four social classes in the Kali age, the phrase 'trade and craft' is stated.
Thus.

children.text: yadi śūdrasyāpi kṛṣyādikam abhyupagamyeta tarhi tenaiva jīvanasiddheḥ kalau dvijaśuśrūṣā parityājyetyāśaṅkyāha ||
children.translated_text: If agriculture and the like are accepted even for a Śūdra, then, since livelihood is established by that very means, service to the twice-born would be abandoned in the Kali age; anticipating this objection, he says:
Thus.
Because agriculture and the like are a cause of a more distinguished livelihood through greater gain, they are called vikarman, secondary occupations.

children.text: dvijaśuśrūṣayā tu jīrṇavastrādikam eva labhyate iti na lābhādhikyam ||
children.translated_text: By service to the twice-born, however, only old clothes and the like are obtained; therefore there is no greater gain.

children.text: ato 'dhikalipsayā kṛṣyādikameva kurvanto yadi dvijaśuśrūṣāṃ parityajeyustadā teṣāmaihikam āmuṣmikaṃ ca hīyeta ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, if, from a desire for greater gain, they were to abandon service to the twice-born while engaging only in agriculture and the like, then their welfare in this world and the next would decline.

children.text: itthaṃ varṇacatuṣṭayasādhāraṇaṃ jīvanahetuṃ dharmaṃ pratipādya nigamayati ||
children.translated_text: Having thus set forth the <s>dharma</s> that is the means of livelihood common to the four varṇas, he concludes.

children.text: atīteṣvapi kaliyugeṣu viprādīnāṃ kṛṣyādikam astīti sūcayituṃ sanātanaḥ ityuktam ||
children.translated_text: The word "eternal" is used to indicate that agriculture and the like existed for Brahmins and the others even in past Kali ages.

children.text: yadyapi smṛtyantareṣvivātrāpi varṇadharmānantaram āśramadharmā vaktumucitāḥ tathāpi vyāsenāpṛṣṭatvād ācāryeṇopekṣitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although, here too, after the duties of the varṇas it would be proper to state the duties of the āśramas, as in other smṛtis, nevertheless the teacher passed them over because <s>Vyāsa</s> had not asked about them.
But we shall describe them too for the benefit of the hearers.

children.text: na ca pūrvādhyāya eva kuto na varṇitā iti mantavyam ||
children.translated_text: Nor should it be thought: why were they not described in the preceding chapter itself?
Because there was no occasion for them there.

children.text: atra tu cāturvarṇyāśramāgatam ityāśramaśabdena teṣāṃ buddhisthatvādasti prasaṅgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, however, since by the word āśrama in the phrase "pertaining to the four varṇas and āśramas" they have entered the mind, there is an occasion.
And those āśramas are of four kinds.
This is said in the <s>Skanda</s>:
The brahmacārin, the householder, the forest-dweller, and then the mendicant:
these, in order, are the four distinct āśramas of Brahmins.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> too says:
The brahmacārin, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the renunciant:
these four distinct āśramas arise from the householder.
Thus.
"Arise from the householder" means "serve the purposes of the householder."
Among them, one consecrated by upanayana is a brahmacārin.
"Lead me near the vow of brahmacarya, to which I have come."
Thus.
This is from the wording of the mantra.
The meaning is: "Lead me, who have come, near for the sake of brahmacarya."

children.text: upanayanaṃ ca garbhādhānādiṣu paṭhitatvāt brāhmaḥ saṃskāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: And upanayana, since it is listed among rites beginning with garbhādhāna, is a brāhma saṃskāra.
<s>Hārīta</s> states this:

children.text: dvividho hi saṃskāro bhavati brāhmo daivaśca
children.translated_text: For saṃskāra is of two kinds: brāhma and daiva.
The smārta rite beginning with garbhādhāna is brāhma.
The pākayajñas, haviryajñas, and soma rites are daiva.

children.text: brāhmeṇa saṃskṛta ṛṣīṇāṃ samānatāṃ sāyujyaṃ gacchati
children.translated_text: One consecrated by the brāhma rite attains equality and union with the seers.

children.text: daivenottareṇa saṃskṛto devānāṃ samānatāṃ sāyujyaṃ gacchati ||
children.translated_text: Consecrated by the further daiva rite, he attains equality and union with the gods.
Thus.
The rites beginning with garbhādhāna are enumerated by <s>Gautama</s>:
Garbhādhāna, puṃsavana, anavalobhana, sīmantonnayana, jātakarman, nāmakaraṇa, annaprāśana, caula, and upanayana;
the four Vedic vows;
the bath and union with a wife who shares one's <s>dharma</s>;
the performance of the five sacrifices, namely to gods, ancestors, humans, beings, and brahman; and, among these,

children.text: aṣṭakā pārvaṇaśrāddhaṃ śrāvaṇyāgrahāyaṇī caitryāśvayujī ceti sapta pākayajñasaṃsthāḥ
children.translated_text: the aṣṭakā, the pārvaṇa śrāddha, the śrāvaṇī, āgrahāyaṇī, caitrī, and āśvayujī: these are the seven institutions of the pākayajña;

children.text: agnyādheyo 'gnihotraṃ darśapūrṇamāsāgrayaṇacāturmāsyāni nirūḍhapaśubandhāḥ sautrāmaṇīti sapta haviryajñasaṃsthāḥ
children.translated_text: the setting up of the sacred fires, agnihotra, darśapūrṇamāsa, āgrayaṇa, cāturmāsya rites, nirūḍhapaśubandha, and sautrāmaṇī: these are the seven institutions of the haviryajña;

children.text: agniṣṭomo 'tyagniṣṭoma ukthyaḥ ṣoḍaśī vājapeyo 'tirātrāptoryāma iti sapta somasaṃsthāḥ
children.translated_text: agniṣṭoma, atyagniṣṭoma, ukthya, ṣoḍaśin, vājapeya, atirātra, and aptoryāma: these are the seven soma institutions.
These are the forty saṃskāras.
Thus.
Among them, the saṃskāras beginning with garbhādhāna and ending with cūḍā are for removing defects produced by seed and womb.

children.text: ata eva yājñavalkyaḥ cūḍāntān saṃskārān nirūpyāha
children.translated_text: For this very reason, after setting forth the saṃskāras ending with cūḍā, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> says:
In this way the sin arising from seed and womb comes to pacification.
Thus.
Therefore they are described before the brahmacarya āśrama.
Among these, for the twice-born, garbhādhāna and the following rites are to be performed with mantras.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states this:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are the varṇas, but the first three are twice-born.
For them the rites from conception to the cremation ground are indeed performed with mantras.
Thus.
The same authority states the particular time for garbhādhāna and the other rites:

children.text: garbhādhānam ṛtau puṃsaḥ savanaṃ spandanāt purā
children.translated_text: Garbhādhāna is in the season; puṃsavana for a male before movement in the womb;

children.text: ṣaṣṭhe'ṣṭame vā sīmanto māsyete jātakarma ca ||
children.translated_text: sīmanta in the sixth or eighth month; and jātakarman in that very month.
Naming is on the eleventh day; going out is in the fourth month;
annaprāśana is in the sixth month; cūḍā is to be performed according to family custom.
Thus.
Beginning with the day on which menstruation is seen, sixteen days are the season.
<s>Manu</s> states this:

children.text: ṛtuḥ svābhāvikaḥ strīṇāṃ rātrayaḥ ṣoḍaśa smṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: The natural season of women is remembered as sixteen nights,
together with four other days, censured by the virtuous.
Of those, the first four, the censured eleventh,

children.text: trayodaśī ca śeṣāḥ syuḥ praśastā daśa rātrayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the thirteenth are excluded; the remaining ten nights are praised.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on odd nights;

children.text: tasmād yugmāsu putrārthī saṃviśed ārtave striyam ||
children.translated_text: therefore one desiring a son should approach his wife in her season on even nights.
Thus.
Here, beginning from the sight of menstruation, four days are censured by the virtuous.
"On even nights" means on even-numbered nights.
"He should approach" means he should go to her.
Thus ends garbhādhāna.
Now puṃsavana.

children.text: evam ṛtau garbhādhānaṃ kṛtvā garbhacalanāt purā puṃsavanaṃ kāryam ||
children.translated_text: Having thus performed garbhādhāna in the season, puṃsavana should be performed before the movement of the fetus.

children.text: taccalanaṃ dvitīye vā tṛtīye vā bhavati ||
children.translated_text: That movement occurs either in the second or in the third month.
<s>Baijavāpa</s> states this:

children.text: māsi dvitīye vā tṛtīye vā purā spandate ||
children.translated_text: In the second or third month, before it moves.
Thus.
<s>Pāraskara</s> also says:
In the second or third month.
On the day when the moon is joined with a male nakṣatra.
Thus.
And the male nakṣatras, beginning with Hasta, are well known in jyotiḥśāstra.
Anavalobhana is to be understood from the <s>Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa</s>.
Thus ends puṃsavana.
Now sīmantonnayana.
Other times for sīmantonnayana, besides the time stated by <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, have also been shown by the sages.
There <s>Laugākṣi</s> says:
In the third month of pregnancy, the sīmantonnayana is to be performed.
Thus.
<s>Āpastamba</s> also says:
In the case of the first pregnancy, in the fourth month.
Thus.
<s>Baijavāpa</s> also says:

children.text: atha sīmantonnayanaṃ caturthe pañcame ṣaṣṭhe vāpi ||
children.translated_text: Now the sīmantonnayana is to be performed in the fourth, fifth, or sixth month.
Thus.
In the <s>Sāṃkhyāyana-gṛhya</s> also:
In the seventh month, in the case of the first pregnancy, the sīmantonnayana is performed.
Thus.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> also says:
The sīmantonnayana is to be performed when the fetus stirs, or so long as delivery has not occurred.
Thus.
Since no specific restriction is heard, all these alternatives are optional.

children.text: etacca sīmantonnayanaṃ kṣetrasaṃskāratvāt sakṛdeva kartavyaṃ na pratigarbham ||
children.translated_text: And this sīmantonnayana, because it is a consecration of the field, is to be performed only once, not for each pregnancy.
And accordingly <s>Hārīta</s> says:
Women of the twice-born, once consecrated by the sīmanta rite, have received that consecration.
Thus.
<s>Devala</s> also says:

children.text: yā sakṛt saṃskṛtā nārī sarvagarbheṣu saṃskṛtā ||
children.translated_text: A woman who has once been consecrated is consecrated in all pregnancies.
Thus.
But on the view that it is a consecration of the fetus, it must be repeated for each pregnancy.
And accordingly <s>Viṣṇu</s> says:
The rite of sīmantonnayana is not regarded as a consecration of the woman;
some, because it consecrates the fetus, apply it to each and every fetus.
Between these two views, the determination is according to one's own gṛhya text.
In the case of the delivery of a woman for whom sīmantonnayana has not been performed, <s>Satyavrata</s> says:
If a woman for whom sīmantonnayana has not been performed should somehow give birth,
then, having taken up the son, she is entitled to the rite of consecration again, according to rule.
Thus ends sīmantonnayana.
Now jātakarma.
There, the time for jātakarma is shown by <s>Yājñavalkya</s>:
And jātakarma when these months have arrived.
Thus.
Here, 'these have arrived' means 'when the child has been born.'
<s>Viṣṇu</s> also says:

children.text: jātakarma tataḥ kuryāt putre jāte yathoditam ||
children.translated_text: Then, when a son has been born, he should perform jātakarma as prescribed.
Thus.
The remainder to be supplied is, 'in his own gṛhya text.'
And that is to be done after bathing.
And accordingly <s>Saṃvarta</s> says:

children.text: jāte putre pituḥ snānaṃ sacailaṃ tu vidhīyate ||
children.translated_text: When a son is born, bathing by the father, together with his clothes, is prescribed.
Thus.
And jātakarma is to be performed before the cutting of the navel-string.
And accordingly <s>Manu</s> says:
Before the cutting of the navel-string, jātakarma is prescribed for a male child,
with mantras, and his feeding with gold, honey, and ghee.
Thus.
'Cutting' means severing.
Nor should it be said that, because of the concern about impurity, there is no eligibility for the rite.
For before the cutting of the navel-string there is no impurity.
<s>Jaimini</s> says this:
So long as the cord is not cut, birth-impurity does not take hold;

children.text: chinne nāle tataḥ paścāt sūtakaṃ tu vidhīyate ||
children.translated_text: after the cord has been cut, then birth-impurity is prescribed.
Thus.
In the <s>Viṣṇudharmottara</s>:
At the birth of a son, a śrāddha is indeed to be performed while the navel-string is uncut;
or else, by self-controlled men, it is to be performed when the impurity has ceased.
Thus.
And that śrāddha is to be performed with a substance of gold.
<s>Vyāsa</s> says this:
When there is lack of materials, lack of Brahmins, absence from home, the birth of a son,
or when one's wife is menstruating, one should perform a gold-śrāddha.
Thus.
In the <s>Ādityapurāṇa</s>, the prohibition of cooked food is shown:
At a birth-śrāddha one should not give cooked food even to Brahmins,
because their purification comes from a cāndrāyaṇa penance, and not otherwise.
Thus.
On that day, gifts should be made according to one's ability.
This is said in the <s>Ādipurāṇa</s>:
The gods and the ancestors, when a son is born to twice-born men,

children.text: āyānti tasmāttadahaḥ puṇyaṃ pūjyaṃ ca sarvadā ||
children.translated_text: come there; therefore that day is always meritorious and worthy of honor.

children.text: tatra dadyāt suvarṇaṃ tu bhūmiṃ gāṃ turagaṃ ratham
children.translated_text: On that occasion one should give gold, land, a cow, a horse, and a chariot.
Thus.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> also says:
To all one's kinsmen one should give bipeds, quadrupeds, grain, gold, and the like.
Thus.
And this is to be done even in the midst of impurity.

children.text: āśauce tu samutpanne putrajanma yadā bhavet
children.translated_text: But when impurity has arisen and the birth of a son takes place,
there is immediate purity for the performer; he becomes pure when the earlier impurity ends.
Thus ends jātakarma.
Now nāmakaraṇa, the naming ceremony.

children.text: tasya ca yājñavalkyoktakālād anye 'pi kālā manunā darśitāḥ
children.translated_text: And for it, besides the time stated by <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, other times also are shown by <s>Manu</s>:

children.text: nāmadheyaṃ daśamyāṃ tu dvādaśyāṃ vāsya kārayet
children.translated_text: He should have the name-giving done on the tenth day, or on the twelfth day for him,

children.text: puṇye tithau muhūrte vā nakṣatre vā guṇānvite ||
children.translated_text: or on an auspicious lunar day, at an auspicious muhūrta, or under a nakṣatra endowed with good qualities.
Thus.
In 'he should have it done,' the causative suffix ṇic is used in the sense of one's own action.
After that, the father himself should give the name on the tenth day.
Thus, from the statement of the <s>Viṣṇupurāṇa</s>.
Or, in the absence or incapacity of the father, he may have it done by another.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> says this:
The father, or another elder of the family, should make the connection with the family deity and the nakṣatra.
Thus.
In the <s>Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa</s>:
Some desire the name-giving on the tenth day, O king,

children.text: dvādaśyāmatha vā rātrau māse pūrṇe tathāpare ||
children.translated_text: or else on the twelfth day, at night, and others when a month has been completed.
Other wise men say it is on the eighteenth day.
Thus.
In the <s>Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa</s> also:

children.text: jananād daśarātre vyuṣṭe saṃvatsare vā nāmakaraṇam ||
children.translated_text: When ten nights have passed from birth, or after a year, the naming ceremony is performed.
Thus.
There the determination is according to one's own gṛhya text.
And <s>Manu</s> shows the form of a name according to the distinction of social class:
For a Brahmin it should be auspicious; for a Kṣatriya, endowed with strength;
for a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but for a Śūdra, contemptible.
For a Brahmin it should have 'śarman'; for a king, be connected with protection;
for a Vaiśya, connected with prosperity; for a Śūdra, connected with service.
For women it should be pleasant to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, charming,
auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and having the expression of a blessing.
Thus.
'Auspicious' and the others are the first elements of the name.
'Śarman' and the others are the final elements.

children.text: tayā ca nāmānyevaṃvidhāni sampadyante śrīśarmā vikramapālaḥ māṇikyaśreṣṭhī hīnadāsaḥ ityādi ||
children.translated_text: And by it names of this kind are obtained: <s>Śrīśarmā</s>, <s>Vikramapāla</s>, <s>Māṇikyaśreṣṭhī</s>, <s>Hīnadāsa</s>, and so on.
But for women, <s>Śrīdāsī</s> and the like.
The meaning is that it is easy to pronounce pleasantly.
On this point <s>Baijavāpa</s> states a special rule:

children.text: pitā nāma karotyekākṣaraṃ dvyakṣaraṃ tryakṣaraṃ caturakṣaramaparimitaṃ vā ghoṣavad ādyantarantasthaṃ dīrghābhiniṣṭhānāntam ||
children.translated_text: The father makes the name of one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, four syllables, or unlimited syllables, beginning with a voiced sound, having a semivowel within, and ending in a long vowel or an abhiniṣṭhāna.
Thus.

children.text: ayamarthaḥ ghoṣavanti yānyakṣarāṇi vargatṛtīyacaturthāni tānyādau kāryāṇi ||
children.translated_text: This is the meaning: the letters that are voiced, the third and fourth letters of the classes, are to be placed at the beginning.
The semivowels ya, ra, la, and va are to be placed in the middle.
At the end is the abhiniṣṭhāna, the visarga.

children.text: tathā ca bhadrapālo jātavedā ityādi nāma bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly the name becomes <s>Bhadrapāla</s>, <s>Jātavedas</s>, and the like.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> and <s>Likhita</s> state the result of naming in the manner described:

children.text: evaṃ kṛte nāmni śuci tatkulaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: When the name is made thus, that family becomes pure.
Thus.
Thus the naming rite.
Now the first outing.
On that point <s>Manu</s> says:
In the fourth month the child's going out from the house should be performed.
Thus.
On that point <s>Yama</s> states what is to be done:
Then, in the third month, the sight of the sun should be performed,
and in the fourth month the child's sight of the moon should be performed.
Thus.
<s>Laugākṣi</s> also says:
In the third half-month there should be the sight of the sun.
Thus.
In the <s>Purāṇa</s> too:
On the twelfth day, O king, there is the child's going out from the house;

children.text: caturthe māsi kartavyaṃ tathānyeṣāṃ ca saṃmatam ||
children.translated_text: in the fourth month it should be performed, and so too it is approved by others.
Thus.
Here too the arrangement is according to one's own Vedic branch.
Thus the first outing.
Now the first feeding of rice.
On that point <s>Yama</s> says:
After that, in the sixth month, the first feeding of rice should be performed according to rule,

children.text: aṣṭame vāpi kartavyaṃ yacceṣṭaṃ maṅgalaṃ kule ||
children.translated_text: or it may be performed in the eighth month, and whatever auspicious practice is desired in the family.
Thus.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> also says:
The first feeding of rice is in the year; some say at half a year.
Thus.
<s>Laugākṣi</s> says:
The first feeding of rice is in the sixth month, or when teeth have appeared.
Thus.
There <s>Mārkaṇḍeya</s> states a special rule:
In front of the deity, while he is seated on the nurse's lap,
adorned, food should be given to him in a golden vessel.
One should feed him rice pudding mixed with honey, ghee, and gold;
then, after the feeding has been performed, the nurse should release the child from her lap.
Thus.
After the feeding, the test of livelihood is shown by <s>Mārkaṇḍeya</s>:
Then, having placed in front all kinds of implements of crafts,

children.text: śastrāṇi caiva vastrāṇi tataḥ paśyettu lakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: and also weapons and garments, one should then observe the sign.

children.text: prathamaṃ yat spṛśed bālastato bhāṇḍaṃ svayaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: Whichever implement the child touches first by himself,

children.text: jīvikā tasya bālasya tenaiva tu bhaviṣyati ||
children.translated_text: by that very thing the livelihood of that child will be.
Thus the first feeding of rice.
Now the tonsure rite.
On that point <s>Yama</s> says:
Then, when a full year has passed, the cūḍā rite is prescribed;

children.text: dvitīye vā tṛtīye vā kartavyaṃ śrutidarśanāt ||
children.translated_text: or it should be performed in the second or third year, according to the testimony of scripture.
Thus.
<s>Baijavāpa</s> says:
The tonsure is in the third year.
Thus.
<s>Śaṅkha</s> also says:
The cūḍā rite is in the third year,
or in the fifth.
Thus.
<s>Laugākṣi</s> also says:
The tonsure is when most of the third year has passed.
Thus.
<s>Śaunaka</s> also says:
The caula is in the third year, or according to the family dharma.
Thus.
There <s>Laugākṣi</s> states the rule for the topknot according to the difference of seers:
For the <s>Vāsiṣṭhas</s>, the kamuñjā is on the right side;
for the <s>Atris</s> and <s>Kāśyapas</s>, it is on both sides;
the <s>Bhṛgus</s> are shaven-headed;
the <s>Aṅgirases</s> have five topknots;
others keep a śikhā for the sake of adornment,
or according to the family dharma.
Thus.
A kamuñjā is a row of hair.
Here the arrangement is according to one's own Vedic branch.

children.text: atra yathoktāḥ cūḍākaraṇāntā anupanītaviṣayāḥ atastatprasaṅgād anye 'pi kecanānupanītadharmāḥ kathyante ||
children.translated_text: Here the rites described up through tonsure concern one who has not been initiated; therefore, in connection with that, some other dharmas of the uninitiated are also stated.
On that point <s>Gautama</s> says:
Before upanayana, he has free movement, free speech, and free eating.
Thus.
Free movement is going as one wishes.
Free speech is speaking obscenities and the like.
Free eating is eating stale food and the like.
In the <s>Viṣṇupurāṇa</s> too:
With regard to what is edible or inedible, and likewise what is drinkable, what may or may not be spoken, and falsehood,

children.text: asmin kāle na doṣaḥ syāt sa yāvannopanīyate ||
children.translated_text: in this period there is no fault, so long as he has not been initiated.
Thus.
And this eating of inedible things concerns matters other than substances that cause a great sin.
For that very reason there is another smṛti:
There may be free movement, eating, and speech, except for great sin.
Thus.
Just as there is no rule concerning what is edible and inedible and so on, so too there is no other duty such as sipping water.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> says this:

children.text: na hyasya vidyate karma kiṃcid ā mauñjibandhanāt
children.translated_text: For him there is no rite at all until the tying of the muñja grass girdle;

children.text: vṛttyā śūdrasamastāvad yāvad vede na jāyate ||
children.translated_text: until he is born in the Veda, in livelihood he is the same as a Śūdra.
Thus.
<s>Gautama</s> also says:
He becomes one who urinates and defecates wherever occasion permits;

children.text: nāsyācamanakalpo vidyate na brahmābhivyāhared anyatra svadhāninayanāt ||
children.translated_text: there is no rule of sipping water for him, and he should not utter the sacred formula, except at the pouring of svadhā.
Thus.
Thus the tonsure rite.
Now the practice of letters is to be performed.
<s>Mārkaṇḍeya</s> says this:

children.text: prāpte tu pañcame varṣe hyaprasupte janārdane
children.translated_text: But when the fifth year has arrived, while <s>Janārdana</s> is not asleep,
avoiding the sixth lunar day, the first lunar day, and likewise the eighth,
and the empty lunar days, the fifteenth, and the days of Saturn and Mars,

children.text: evaṃ suniścite kāle vidyārambhaṃ tu kārayet ||
children.translated_text: at a time thus well ascertained, one should have the beginning of learning performed.

children.text: pūjayitvā hariṃ lakṣmīṃ devīṃ caiva sarasvatīm
children.translated_text: Having worshipped <s>Hari</s>, <s>Lakṣmī</s>, and also the goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s>
and especially the authors of the sūtras of one's own Vedic school and one's own Vedic lore.

children.text: eteṣāmeva devānāṃ nāmnā tu juhuyāt ghṛtam
children.translated_text: In the names of these very deities one should offer ghee
and worship of the best of twice-born men should also be performed with gifts.
The teacher, seated facing east, with the pupil facing west,
should first teach him, together with well-honored twice-born men.
From then onward one should carefully avoid the days on which study is forbidden:
both eighth lunar days, and at the end of the fortnight three days.
Thus.
Thus ends the section on the saṃskāras from conception through cūḍā.
Now, upanayana.
On this, <s>Manu</s> says:
One should perform the upanayana of a Brahmin in the eighth year from conception,

children.text: garbhād ekādaśe rājño garbhāttu dvādaśe viśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: of a ruler in the eleventh from conception, and of a Vaiśya in the twelfth from conception.
For a Brahmin who desires sacred brilliance it should be done in the fifth year,
for a ruler desiring strength in the sixth, and for a Vaiśya desiring wealth in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not pass beyond the sixteenth year for a Brahmin,

children.text: ā dvāviṃśāt kṣatrabandhor ā catvāriṃśater viśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: beyond the twenty-second for a Kshatriya, or beyond the fortieth for a Vaiśya.
After that, all these three, not having been initiated at the proper time,
become fallen from the Sāvitrī, vrātyas, censured by the Āryas.
With these impure men a Brahmin should never, even in distress,
enter into Brahmanical or marital relations according to rule.
Thus.
<s>Āpastamba</s> also says:

children.text: saptame brahmavarcasakāmamaṣṭama āyuṣkāmaṃ navame tejaskāmaṃ daśame 'nnādyakāmaṃ ekādaśa indriyakāmaṃ dvādaśe paśukāmam ||
children.translated_text: In the seventh year one should initiate one who desires sacred brilliance; in the eighth, one who desires long life; in the ninth, one who desires splendor; in the tenth, one who desires food to eat; in the eleventh, one who desires strength of the senses; in the twelfth, one who desires cattle.
Thus.
And this is common to the three social classes.
He himself states the rule of time according to the arrangement of the classes:

children.text: vasante brāhmaṇamupanayati grīṣme rājanyaṃ śaradi vaiśyam ||
children.translated_text: He initiates a Brahmin in spring, a Kshatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the procedure for upanayana in the order of the social classes:
The brahmacārins should wear black-antelope, ruru-deer, and goat skins,
respectively, and garments of hemp, linen, and wool.
Thus.
The skins beginning with black-antelope are upper garments.
And accordingly <s>Śaṅkha</s> says:
Black-antelope, ruru-deer, and goat skins are the upper garments.
Thus.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> also says:
A black-antelope skin is the upper garment of a Brahmin,
a ruru-deer skin of a Kshatriya,
and a cow skin or goat skin of a Vaiśya.
Thus.
And accordingly <s>Pāraskara</s> says:
An antelope skin is the upper garment of a Brahmin,
a ruru-deer skin of a Kshatriya,

children.text: ājaṃ gavyaṃ vā vaiśyasya sarveṣāṃ vā gavyam ||
children.translated_text: a goat skin or cow skin of a Vaiśya, or a cow skin for all.
Thus.
The garments beginning with hemp are upper garments.
Here <s>Āpastamba</s> says:
The garment:
hemp, linen, and skins;
some prescribe a reddish-brown garment for a Brahmin,
a madder-colored one for a Kshatriya,
and a turmeric-colored one for a Vaiśya.
Thus.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> says:
A white, unworn garment is for a Brahmin,
cotton, madder-colored, or linen for a Kshatriya,
and turmeric-colored or silk for a Vaiśya.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the girdle:

children.text: mauñjī trivṛt samā ślakṣṇā kāryā viprasya mekhalā
children.translated_text: For a Brahmin the girdle should be of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;

children.text: kṣatriyasya tu maurvī jyā vaiśyasya śaṇatāntavī ||
children.translated_text: for a Kshatriya it should be a bowstring of mūrva fiber, and for a Vaiśya made of hemp threads.
Thus.
Triple-stranded means having three cords.
<s>Yama</s> also says:

children.text: viprasya mekhalā mauñjī jyā maurvī kṣatriyasya tu
children.translated_text: The girdle of a Brahmin is of muñja grass, while that of a Kshatriya is a mūrva bowstring;

children.text: śāṇasūtrī tu vaiśyasya mekhalā dharmataḥ smṛtāḥ ||
children.translated_text: the girdle of a Vaiśya is remembered according to dharma as made of hemp thread.
But in the absence even of these, from kuśa grass, aśmantaka, and balvaja,

children.text: mekhalā trivṛtā kāryā granthinaikena vā trivṛt ||
children.translated_text: a triple girdle should be made, or one triple-stranded with a single knot.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> too says:
In the absence of muñja grass, girdles should be made from kuśa grass, aśmantaka, and balvaja,
triple-stranded, with one knot, or indeed with three or five.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the staff:
A Brahmin is entitled, according to dharma, to bilva or palāśa staffs, a Kshatriya to banyan or khadira,
and a Vaiśya to pīlu or udumbara staffs.
Thus.
<s>Yama</s> states the substitute:
But in the absence even of these, for all, woods suitable for every sacrifice may be used.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the measure of the staff:
The Brahmin's staff should reach to the hair, according to measure;
that of the ruler should be level with the forehead, while that of the Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose.
Thus.
<s>Gautama</s> also says:
They are measured by the head, forehead, and tip of the nose.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the characteristics of the staff:
All of them should be straight, without wounds, pleasant to look at,
not alarming to people, with bark, and not damaged by fire.
Thus.
<s>Gautama</s> also says:
Uncrushed, with sacrificial-post-like tops, and with bark.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the sacred thread:
The sacred thread of a Brahmin should be cotton, spun upward, and triple;
that of a ruler should be made of hemp, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen thread.
Thus.
<s>Paiṭhīnasi</s> also says:
The sacred thread of a Brahmin is cotton,
that of a Kshatriya is linen,
and that of a Vaiśya is woolen.
Thus.
When the stated sacred thread is unavailable, cow hair and the like may be taken according to possibility.
<s>Devala</s> states this:
A sacred thread made of cotton, linen, cow hair, hemp, bark, grass, and the like,
should always be made by twice-born men according to what is available.
Thus.
<s>Ṛṣyaśṛṅga</s> says:

children.text: api vā vāsasī yajñopavītārthaṃ kuryāttadabhāve trivṛtā sūtreṇa ||
children.translated_text: Or else he may use two garments for the purpose of the sacred thread; in their absence, with a triple thread.
Thus.
And that should be made with nine filaments.
<s>Devala</s> states this:
One should make the sacred thread with a thread of nine filaments.
Thus.
<s>Kātyāyana</s> says:
It should be triple-stranded and spun upward, with three filaments spun downward.
Thus.
The compiler states the definition of 'spun upward':
With the right hand raised upward, it is made threefold;

children.text: valitaṃ mānavaiḥ sūtraṃ śāstra ūrdhvavṛtaṃ smṛtam ||
children.translated_text: the thread twisted by men is remembered in the śāstra as upward-twisted.
Thus.

children.text: ūrdhvaṃ gatena dakṣiṇena kareṇa yadvalitaṃ tad ūrdhvavṛtam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: what is twisted by the right hand as it goes upward is called upward-twisted.
<s>Devala</s> states the procedure for the yajñopavīta:
Having gone out from the village, one should measure it on ninety-six finger-breadths;
having made the thread threefold to that extent, one should wash it with the three ābliṅga verses.

children.text: devāgāre 'thavā goṣṭhe nadyāṃ vānyatra vā śucau
children.translated_text: In a temple, or in a cow-pen, or in a river, or elsewhere in a clean place,
one should make the new thread threefold with the Sāvitrī; then it becomes a new thread.
One should then tie it to any one of the sacrificial trees, such as bilva or aśvattha;
it should be still living, and one should say, 'Homage to the ancestors.'

children.text: vyāmaṃ nāvekṣitavyaṃ syāt pitṝṇāṃ tṛptidaṃ hi tat
children.translated_text: One should not look at it for a span; for that gives satisfaction to the ancestors.

children.text: tristāḍayet karatalaṃ devānāṃ tṛptidaṃ hi tat ||
children.translated_text: One should strike the palm three times; for that gives satisfaction to the gods.
Taking clay in the left hand, one should place it on this, saying 'bhūḥ';

children.text: patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ vāpi vyāhṛtībhiḥ pratikṣipet ||
children.translated_text: one should cast on a leaf, flower, or fruit with the vyāhṛtis.
Then, having consecrated it with the three recitations of 'bhūr agniḥ' and the rest,
and having bowed to <s>Hari</s>, <s>Brahmā</s>, and <s>Īśvara</s>, one should put it on.
Thus.
The mantra for putting it on is 'yajñopavītam' and so on.
<s>Kātyāyana</s> states the rule about the knot:
The sacred thread should be threefold, and one knot is prescribed for it.
Thus.
The same authority states the measure of the yajñopavīta:

children.text: pṛṣṭhavaṃśe ca nābhyāṃ ca dhṛtaṃ yad vindate kaṭim
children.translated_text: When worn, what reaches from the back-bone and the navel to the waist
is the sacred thread fit to be worn; it should be neither too long nor too high.
Thus.
<s>Devala</s> also says:
It must never be made above the breast or below the navel.
Thus.
<s>Bhṛgu</s> states the number of sacred threads:
For a young student there is one sacred thread; for the other two, two are remembered.

children.text: ekam eva yatīnāṃ syāditi śāstrasya niścayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For renunciants there should be only one: this is the settled conclusion of the śāstra.
Thus.
And this is intended as a daily rule.
Because many are heard of in the case of desire.
<s>Devala</s> says this:
Many are for one who desires long life.
Thus.
This sacred thread is always to be worn.
<s>Bhṛgu</s> says this:
One should always be wearing the sacred thread, and always have the topknot tied.

children.text: viśikho vyupavītaśca yat karoti na tat kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: What one does without a topknot and without a sacred thread is not done.
The wise man who desires his own good should not remove
the yajñopavīta that has been purified by mantra and rests on his body.
By removing it even once, that twice-born man becomes liable to expiation.
Thus.
<s>Devala</s> states a special rule concerning the sacred thread:
If the thread is hairy, then, after making it counter to the hair,
one should sprinkle it ten times with waters consecrated by the Sāvitrī.
If it is broken, or has slipped down, or has been made after eating, one should discard it.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the procedure when the yajñopavīta and the rest are broken:
The girdle, the antelope-skin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot,
when ruined, should be thrown into the waters, and one should take others with mantra.
Thus.
Now, after wearing the staff and the other things, worship of the sun is to be performed.
<s>Manu</s> says so:
Having received the desired staff and having worshipped <s>Bhāskara</s>,
having gone around the fire clockwise, he should go begging for alms according to rule.
Thus.

children.text: daṇḍagrahaṇāntetikartavyatāyuktam upanayanaṃ prāpya gāyatrīmahāvākyārthabhūtaṃ bhāskaramupasthāya so'hamityevaṃ jñātvā agniṃ paricarya bhaikṣyaṃ caredityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: having obtained the upanayana furnished with the duties following the taking of the staff, and having worshipped <s>Bhāskara</s>, who is the meaning of the great sentence of the Gāyatrī, and having known 'I am he' in this way, he should tend the fire and go begging for alms.
The tending of the fire is shown by <s>Manu</s>:
Having brought fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
at evening and morning he should, without negligence, offer them into the fire.
Thus.
The meaning is that he should place them in the open air, in the atmosphere, and not on the ground.
<s>Baijavāpa</s> states a special rule for fetching fuel-sticks:

children.text: purāstamayāt prāgudīcīṃ diśaṃ gatvā ahiṃsannaraṇyāt samidham āharet
children.translated_text: Before sunset, having gone first toward the northern direction, one should bring a fuel-stick from the forest without injuring anything.
One who desires brahmic splendor should bring dry ones; one who desires food should bring moist ones; one who desires both should bring both kinds.
Thus.
<s>Kātyāyana</s> states the characteristics of a fuel-stick:
A fuel-stick should never be thicker than the thumb;

children.text: na viyuktā tvacā caiva na sakīṭā na pāṭitā ||
children.translated_text: it should not be separated from its bark, not worm-eaten, and not split.
It should be neither longer nor shorter than a span, and it should not be forked;

children.text: na saparṇā nātiyāmā homeṣu tu vijānatā ||
children.translated_text: one who knows should understand that in offerings it should not have leaves and should not be overgrown.

children.text: viśīrṇā vimalā hrasvā vakrā sasuṣirā kṛśā
children.translated_text: A decayed, dirty, short, crooked, hollow, thin,
long, or thick stick, defective in its qualities, destroys the success of the rite.
Thus.
The rule for fuel-sticks is stated in the <s>Vāyupurāṇa</s>:
Fuel-sticks should be of palāśa; failing that, of khadira.
In their absence, śamī, rohitaka, and aśvattha; and in their absence, arka and vetasa.
Thus.
<s>Hārīta</s> states the fault in failing to perform the fire-duty:
In former times Death seized a brahmacārin, harming him;
Fire released him. Therefore one should tend that fire.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states the manner of begging for alms:
One should beg for alms among blameless Brahmins for the maintenance of oneself.
It is marked by the word 'bhavat' at the beginning, middle, or end,
for the alms-round of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively.
Thus.
'Among Brahmins' is an indication of those of one's own respective caste.
For this very reason <s>Vyāsa</s> says:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should go begging every day
only in houses of their own caste, or else in houses of all classes.
Thus.
Its applicability to all social classes concerns a case of distress.
For this very reason it is shown in the <s>Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa</s>:
O descendant of <s>Kuru</s>, when there is no obtaining otherwise, one should practice begging among the four classes.
Thus.
Even in distress one should not take cooked food from a Śūdra.
<s>Āṅgirasa</s> says this:
When without livelihood, one may take only uncooked food from the lowest class, enough for one night.

children.text: āmaṃ pūyati saṃsāre dharmyaṃ tebhyaḥ pratiṣṭhitam ||
children.translated_text: Uncooked food purifies in the world; what is lawful is established among them.
Therefore uncooked food is to be accepted even from a Śūdra, said <s>Āṅgirasa</s>.
Thus.
When there is no distress, he should practice begging only among those of his own caste who are commendable.
<s>Manu</s> says this:
From houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, and who are commendable in their own duties,
the brahmacārin, self-controlled, should fetch alms every day.
Thus.
'At the beginning, middle, and end': thus.

children.text: ayamarthaḥ bhikṣāpravartanāvākye varṇakrameṇa ādimadhyāvasāneṣu bhavacchabdaḥ prayojyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is this: in the sentence for setting begging in motion, the word 'bhavat' is to be used at the beginning, middle, and end according to the order of the social classes.
And so <s>Manu</s> says:
After initiation, the best twice-born should beg with 'bhavat' first;
a Rājanya with 'bhavat' in the middle, but a Vaiśya with 'bhavat' at the end.
Thus.
The same author states an exception in certain cases that have been mentioned:

children.text: gurau kule na bhikṣeta na jñātikulabandhuṣu
children.translated_text: He should not beg in the guru's family, nor among relatives, family members, and friends.
But when other houses are unavailable, he should abandon these one after another in the prior order.
Or, if those previously mentioned are impossible, he may go begging through the whole village,
restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, but avoiding those who are accused.
Thus.
But the passage:

children.text: mātaraṃ vā svasāraṃ vā māturvā bhaginīṃ nijām
children.translated_text: From his mother, or his sister, or his own mother's sister,

children.text: bhikṣeta bhikṣāṃ prathamaṃ yā cainaṃ na vimānayet ||
children.translated_text: he should first beg alms, from whichever woman will not disrespect him,
that concerns the begging that forms an auxiliary of the upanayana rite.
And those alms should be brought in an amount sufficient for a meal.
For otherwise a fault is heard of.
<s>Yama</s> says this:
One should nowhere bring alms in excess of the measure of food needed.
A person who deliberately brings more than that is joined with the fault of theft.
Thus.
And those alms are to be eaten after first obtaining the guru's permission.
<s>Manu</s> and <s>Yama</s> say this:
Having collected those alms honestly, according to what is needed,
he should present them to the guru and eat, after sipping water, pure and facing east.
Thus.
When the guru is absent, he should present them to the guru's wife and the others.
<s>Gautama</s> says this:
Having presented them to the guru, and having been permitted, he eats.
In the guru's absence, he presents them to the guru's wife, sons, or fellow brahmacārins.
Thus.
Alms permitted by the guru should be eaten with respect.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> says this:
Having performed the fire rite, he should eat, restrained in speech, with the guru's permission,
after first performing the water-sipping rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.
Thus.
And the honoring is shown by <s>Hārīta</s>:

children.text: bhaikṣyamavekṣitaṃ paryagnikṛtam ādityadarśitaṃ gurave niveditam anujñātam amṛtasaṃmitaṃ prāhuḥ
children.translated_text: Alms that have been looked upon, passed around the fire, shown to the sun, presented to the guru, and permitted are said to be equal to nectar.
When the brahmacārin eats them, he obtains perfection in sacred knowledge.
Thus.
<s>Gautama</s> also says:
In the evening and in the morning he should eat food that has been honored, without disparaging it.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> states the prohibition against eating from a single person's food:
The vow-observer should always live by alms; he should not be one who eats from a single source.
The livelihood of one under a vow through alms is remembered as equal to fasting.
When asked, he may eat as he wishes at a rite for the gods, a rite for the ancestors, or a rite for seers, as in the case of a vow.
His vow is not thereby broken.
Thus.
The same author states the demerit if this is not done:
Without having gone begging and without having kindled the fire,
if he is not ill, for seven nights he should perform the avakīrṇin vow.
Thus.
<s>Yama</s> states the rule for one who has been initiated:

children.text: daṇḍaṃ kamaṇḍaluṃ vedaṃ mauñjīṃ ca raśanāṃ tathā
children.translated_text: He should carry a staff, a water-pot, the Veda, the muñja girdle, and likewise a belt,
and he should maintain brahmacarya, eating food obtained by begging and living with the guru.
Thus.
'Veda' means a handful of darbha grass.
'With the guru' means in the guru's house.
<s>Yama</s> says:
The brahmacārin should always wear the girdle, antelope skin, staff, and sacred thread,

children.text: kaupīnaṃ kaṭisūtraṃ ca brahmacārī ca dhārayet ||
children.translated_text: and also a loincloth and waist-cord.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> says:
Kindling the fire, going for alms, sleeping on the ground, and what is beneficial to the guru,
the twice-born who has undergone upanayana should do until his return home from studentship.
Thus.
<s>Sumantu</s> also says:
Brahmacarya, austerity, begging, the fire rite at the two twilights,
Vedic recitation, and conduct toward the guru: this is the practice of a brahmacārin.
Thus.
<s>Vyāsa</s> states the manner of conduct toward the guru:
In the guru's house he should be one who lies down last and rises first.

children.text: yacca śiṣyeṇa kartavyaṃ yacca dāsena vā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is to be done by a pupil, or again by a servant,

children.text: kṛtam ityeva tat sarvaṃ kṛtvā tiṣṭhettu pārśvataḥ
children.translated_text: having done all that, simply saying 'it has been done,' he should stand nearby,
as an attendant, doing every task and skilled in all duties.
He should not eat when the guru has not eaten; he should not drink when the guru has not drunk.

children.text: na tiṣṭhati tathāsīta nāsupte prasvapet tathā ||
children.translated_text: He should not sit while the guru is standing, nor should he sleep while the guru has not slept.
Thus.
<s>Viśvāmitra</s> says:
Toward the guru's wife and son, and toward elders who are devoted to dharma,
service should always be performed, with prostrations and the like.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states the things to be avoided:
Honey, meat, collyrium, leftovers, sour substances, women, injury to living beings,
looking at the sun, obscene speech, slander, and the like he should avoid.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> also says:

children.text: varjayenmadhu māṃsaṃ ca gandhaṃ mālyaṃ rasān striyaḥ
children.translated_text: He should avoid honey and meat, perfumes, garlands, flavorful foods, and women,

children.text: śuktāni yāni sarvāṇi prāṇināṃ caiva hiṃsanam ||
children.translated_text: all sour substances, and also injury to living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, and wearing shoes or carrying an umbrella

children.text: kāmaṃ krodhaṃ ca lobhaṃ ca nartanaṃ gītavādanam ||
children.translated_text: Desire, anger, and greed, dancing, singing, and instrumental music,

children.text: dyūtaṃ ca janavādaṃ ca parīvādaṃ tathānṛtam
children.translated_text: gambling, public gossip, slander, and also falsehood,
gazing at women and taking support from them, and injury to another,

children.text: ekaḥ śayīta sarvatra na retaḥ skandayet kvacit ||
children.translated_text: he should sleep alone everywhere, and should never emit semen.
Thus.
<s>Yama</s>:
He should avoid a bed, a seat, lying down on a bed, and cleaning the teeth.

children.text: svapedekaḥ kuśeṣveva na retaḥ skandayet śuciḥ ||
children.translated_text: Being pure, he should sleep alone only on kuśa grass, and should not emit semen.
Thus.
In the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>:
He should not look into a mirror, and should not practice cleaning the teeth.
He may use the teacher's leftovers for the sake of medicine, not out of desire.
Thus.
<s>Āpastamba</s> also says:
The leftovers of one's father and of one's eldest brother should be eaten.
Thus.
But the leftovers of the teacher's son and others should not be eaten.
<s>Manu</s> says this:
Rubbing the limbs, bathing, and eating leftovers,
he should not do for the teacher's son, nor should he wash his feet.
Anointing, bathing, and rubbing the limbs,

children.text: gurupatnyā na kāryāṇi keśānāṃ ca prasādhanam ||
children.translated_text: and arranging the hair should not be done for the teacher's wife.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states the limit of the period of brahmacarya:
For each Veda, brahmacarya lasts twelve years, or five,
or until the completion of study, according to some; and the keśānta rite is in the sixteenth year.
Thus.
Keśānta is the rite called godāna.
And that is to be performed in the sixteenth year.
<s>Manu</s> says this:
The keśānta is prescribed in the sixteenth year for a Brahmin,
in the twenty-second for one belonging to the royal class, and for a Vaiśya two years beyond that.
Thus.
<s>Yama</s>:

children.text: vased dvādaśa varṣāṇi caturviṃśatim eva vā
children.translated_text: He should live for twelve years, or indeed for twenty-four,

children.text: ṣaṭtriṃśataṃ vā varṣāṇi prativedaṃ vrataṃ caret ||
children.translated_text: or for thirty-six years, and should observe the vow for each Veda.
Thus.
This is intended with reference to the study of the three Vedas.
For that very reason <s>Manu</s> says:
The vow with the teacher for the three Vedas lasts thirty-six years,
or half of that, or a quarter of that, or simply until the completion of study.
Thus.
The brahmacārin characterized in this way is of two kinds.
There is the upakurvāṇaka and the naiṣṭhika.
The duties of the upakurvāṇaka have been stated.
Those of the naiṣṭhika are now stated.
On this <s>Yājñavalkya</s> says:
But the naiṣṭhika brahmacārin should live in the presence of the teacher;
in his absence, with his son, with his wife, or even with the Vaiśvānara fire.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> also says:

children.text: yadi tvātyantiko vāso rocetāsya guroḥ kule
children.translated_text: But if permanent residence in the teacher's family pleases him,
being disciplined, he should attend upon him until the release of the body.

children.text: ācārye tu khalu prete guruputre guṇānvite
children.translated_text: When the teacher has died, he should behave as toward the teacher toward the teacher's son, if endowed with virtues,
or toward the teacher's wife, or toward a sapiṇḍa relative of the teacher.
When these are not present, being one whose habits are standing, sitting, and moving about,
practicing service to the fire, he should bring his own body to completion.
Thus.
And this concerns a virtuous Brahmin teacher and the like.
Otherwise there is fault.
This was stated by that very authority:
A student should not live in permanent residence with a non-Brahmin teacher,
nor with a Brahmin who has not studied, if he desires the highest goal.
Thus.
<s>Vasiṣṭha</s> also says:
A brahmacārin should attend upon the teacher until the release of the body.
And when the teacher dies, he should attend upon the fire,
restrained in speech,
eating at every fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time,
practicing begging,
dependent on the teacher,
wearing matted hair, or a topknot with matted hair.

children.text: guruṃ gacchantamanugacchannāsīnaṃ cettiṣṭhan śayānaṃ ced āsīna upāsīta
children.translated_text: When the teacher is going, he should follow him; when he is seated, he should stand; when he is lying down, he should sit near him.
He studies when called.
Having reported everything he has obtained, he eats with the teacher's permission.
He avoids beds, lying on beds, cleaning the teeth, washing, collyrium, anointing, shoes, and an umbrella.
His habit is standing and sitting; three times a day he should approach the waters.
Thus.
The meaning is that he should bathe at the three junctions of the day.
Service to the fire has been described by <s>Hārīta</s>, <s>Śaṅkha</s>, <s>Likhita</s>, and <s>Yama</s>:

Having brought sacrificial firewood, he should attend upon the fire with sweeping, smearing, awakening, gathering, kindling, carrying fire around, circumambulation, attendance, oblation, praise, homage, and the like.
He should not step over the fire.
He should not drag it with his feet.
He should not blow on it with his mouth.
He should not carry water and fire at the same time.
He should not place fuel on it when he has eaten with undigested food in him, or when he is in a state of leftovers.
Day by day he should kindle the fire with various special oblations belonging to Agni.
He should go after taking leave.
Having brought something, he should report it, with his mind fixed on that.
At the end, when the body ceases, he attains union with Brahman.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states the fruit for one who acts thus:
Subduing his body by this rule, with his senses conquered,
he obtains Brahmaloka and is not born again here.
Thus.
<s>Manu</s> also says:

children.text: ā samāpteḥ śarīrasya yastu śuśrūṣate gurum
children.translated_text: The Brahmin who serves the teacher until the completion of the body

children.text: sa gacchatyañjasā vipro brahmaṇaḥ sadma śāśvatam ||
children.translated_text: goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahman.
Thus.
But, it may be objected, if lifelong brahmacarya is accepted, the householder state would have no object.
That is not so.
For the householder state has as its object those who are subject to passion.
<s>Jābāli</s> says this:

children.text: yadi gṛhameva kāmayettadā yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt ||
children.translated_text: If one desires a household, then one should offer the agnihotra for as long as one lives.
Thus.

children.text: atra kecit naiṣṭhikabrahmacaryaṃ kubjādiviṣayaṃ manvānā gārhasthyasya taditaraviṣayatāmāhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here some, thinking that lifelong brahmacarya applies to hunchbacks and the like, say that the householder state applies to those other than them.
And they cite there the statement of <s>Viṣṇu</s>:
For hunchbacks, dwarfs, those blind from birth, impotent men, the lame, the afflicted, and the diseased,
their observance of the vow lasts for life, without doubt.
Thus.
That is not so.

children.text: naiṣṭhikabrahmacaryasya kubjādiṣveva niyatatve samarthaṃ pratyaicchikatvam ucyamānaṃ virudhyeta ||
children.translated_text: If lifelong brahmacarya were restricted only to the hunchbacked and the like, then the optionality being stated with respect to a capable person would be contradicted.
And its optional character is shown by <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>.
There are four āśramas: brahmacārin, householder, forest-dweller, and renunciant.

children.text: teṣāṃ vedam adhītya vedau vedān vāviśīrṇabrahmacaryo yamicchettamāvaset ||
children.translated_text: Of these, after studying one Veda, two Vedas, or the Vedas, with his brahmacarya unbroken, he should enter whichever one he desires.
Thus.
Also in the <s>Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa</s>:
O king, if he desires householdership, he should take a wife;
or he should pass his time in brahmacarya, with prior resolve.
Or he may become a Vaikhānasa, or else a renunciant, according to his desire.
Thus.
Therefore householdership must be established only as applying to one who has attachment.
Thus ends the section on the brahmacārin.

children.text: atha gṛhasthāśramaṃ nirūpayituṃ tadadhikārahetu snānam ādau nirūpyate ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to explain the householder āśrama, the bath, which is the cause of eligibility for it, is first explained.
On this <s>Yājñavalkya</s> says:

children.text: gurave tu varaṃ dattvā snāyīta tadanujñayā
children.translated_text: Having given the chosen gift to the guru, he should bathe with his permission,

children.text: vedaṃ vratāni vā pāraṃ nītvā hyubhayameva vā ||
children.translated_text: after bringing the Veda, the vows, or both of them to completion.
Thus.
There the gift that is to be given is shown by <s>Manu</s>.

children.text: na pūrvaṃ gurave kiṃcid upakurvīta dharmavit
children.translated_text: One who knows dharma should not previously render anything to the guru;
but when he is about to bathe and has been instructed by the guru, he should bring what serves the guru, according to his capacity.
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, shoes, a seat,

children.text: dhānyaṃ vāsāṃsi śākaṃ vā gurave prītim āvahet ||
children.translated_text: grain, garments, vegetables, or whatever brings satisfaction to the guru.
Thus.

children.text: ayaṃ ca varo guruprītyartho na tu vidyāniṣkrayārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And this gift is for pleasing the guru, not for paying the price of knowledge.
For there can be no price adequate to the knowledge of the Veda.
So too the <s>Chāndoga</s> śruti says:
