children.text: yadyapyasmā imām adbhiḥ parigṛhītāṃ dhanasya pūrṇāṃ dadyād etadeva tato bhūyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Even if one were to give him this earth, surrounded by waters and filled with wealth, this alone would be greater than that.
Thus.
The <s>Tāpanīya</s> śruti also says:
The earth with its seven continents is not sufficient as dakṣiṇā.
Thus.
The <s>Hārītasmṛti</s> also says:
If a guru teaches even a single syllable to a pupil,

children.text: pṛthivyāṃ nāsti tad dravyaṃ yad dattvā tvanṛṇī bhavet ||
children.translated_text: there is no substance on earth by giving which he could become free of debt.
Thus.

children.text: vā vedaṃ vratāni ityanena snātakatraividhyaṃ darśitam ||
children.translated_text: By the words "the Veda, the vows, or both," the threefold distinction of snātakas is shown.
Among them, one who completes only the Veda is the first.
One who completes only the vow is the second.
One who completes both is the third.
By the word "vow" here are intended the vows well known in the gṛhya tradition: the upanayana vow, the Sāvitrī vow, and the Veda vows.
The threefold distinction of snātakas is stated by <s>Hārīta</s>.
There are three snātakas:
the snātaka in knowledge, the snātaka in vows, and the snātaka in both knowledge and vows.
Thus.

children.text: vedaṃ pāraṃ nītvety atrārthāvagatir api vivakṣitā ||
children.translated_text: In the phrase "having brought the Veda to the far shore," understanding its meaning is also intended.
For this very reason, in the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>:

children.text: vedaṃ vedau tathā vedān vedān vā caturo dvijaḥ
children.translated_text: A twice-born man, having studied one Veda, two Vedas, the Vedas, or all four Vedas,
and having understood the meaning, should then bathe, O best of the twice-born.
Thus.
And the manner of the bath is well known in the gṛhya texts.
The duties of a snātaka are shown in the <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>:
Two sacred threads, a water-filled water-pot,
an umbrella, a spotless turban, sandals, and shoes;

children.text: raukme ca kuṇḍale vedaṃ kṛttakeśanakhaḥ śuciḥ
children.translated_text: golden earrings and the Veda; with hair and nails cut, pure,

children.text: svādhyāye nityayuktaḥ syād bahirmālyaṃ ca dhārayet ||
children.translated_text: he should be constantly devoted to self-study and should wear an outer garland.
He should always wear white clothing, be fragrant, and be pleasant to look at.
When he has the means, he should not wear old or dirty clothing.

children.text: na raktamulbaṇaṃ cānyadhṛtaṃ vāso na kanthikām
children.translated_text: Nor should he wear red, excessive, or another person’s garment, nor a patched rag.
Thus.
Thus ends the section on the snātaka.
Now, marriage.
On this <s>Manu</s> says:
Having bathed with the guru’s permission and returned home according to rule,
a twice-born man should marry a wife of the same varṇa, endowed with the proper marks.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> also says:
With brahmacarya unimpaired, he should marry a woman having auspicious marks,
one not previously given to another, lovely, not a sapiṇḍa, and younger than himself.
She should be healthy, have brothers, and not belong to the same ārṣa gotra.
Thus.
"Having auspicious marks" means endowed with both external and internal marks.
The external marks are shown by <s>Manu</s>.
He should marry a woman whose limbs are without defect, whose name is gentle, who walks like a goose or an elephant,
whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
Thus.
The same authority states those who are to be avoided:

children.text: nodvahet kapilāṃ kanyāṃ nādhikāṅgīṃ na rogiṇīm
children.translated_text: He should not marry a tawny girl, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased,

children.text: nālomikāṃ nātilomāṃ na vācālāṃ na piṅgalām ||
children.translated_text: nor one without body hair, nor one with too much body hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.
Nor one named after a constellation, tree, or river, nor one named after an outcaste or a mountain,
nor one named after a bird, snake, or servant, nor one with a frightening name.
Thus.
Kapilā means one the color of red rice.
Piṅgalā means fire-colored.
"Outcaste" means one with a mleccha name.
Also in the <s>Viṣṇupurāṇa</s>:
A wise man should not marry a woman who has signs of a beard, nor one with a masculine form,

children.text: na ghargharasvarāṃ kṣāmāṃ tathā kākasvarāṃ na ca ||
children.translated_text: nor one with a rattling voice, one emaciated, or one with a crow-like voice.
Likewise he should not marry one whose eyes are unsteady, nor one with round eyes,
nor one whose shanks are hairy and whose ankles are raised.

children.text: gaṇḍayoḥ kūpakau yasyā hasantyāstāṃ ca nodvahet
children.translated_text: Nor should he marry one who has dimples in her cheeks when she laughs,
nor one whose complexion is very rough, nor one with pale, dusty, or reddish eyes.
A wise man should not marry a girl with swollen hands and feet,
nor one who is dwarfish, nor one who is excessively tall, nor one whose eyebrows meet.
Nor should a man marry one with teeth set too far apart, nor one with a terrible face.
Thus.
But the internal marks are stated in the <s>Āśvalāyana Gṛhya</s>.
The marks are difficult to know.

children.text: aṣṭau piṇḍān kṛtvā ṛtam agre prathamaṃ jajña ṛte satyaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ yad iyaṃ kumāryabhijātā tadiyamiha pratipadyatāṃ yatsatyaṃ tad dṛśyatāmiti piṇḍān abhimantrya kumārīṃ brūyād eṣām ekaṃ gṛhāṇeti
children.translated_text: Having made eight balls, one should first consecrate the balls with the mantra, "Ṛta was born first in the beginning; on ṛta truth is established. Since this maiden has been born here, let her attain that here; let what is truth be seen," and should say to the maiden, "Take one of these."

children.text: kṣetrācced ubhayataḥ sasyād gṛhṇīyād annavatyasyāḥ prajā bhaviṣyatīti vidyāt
children.translated_text: If she takes one from a field producing crops on both sides, one should know, "Her offspring will be endowed with food."
If from a cow-pen, she will be endowed with cattle.
If from the soil of the altar, she will possess brahmic splendor.
If from a lake that is not drying up, she will be endowed with every prosperity.
If from gambling, she will be a gambler.
If from a crossroads, she will wander away from Brahmins.
If from barren ground, she will be without wealth.
If from a cremation ground, she will kill her husband.
Thus.

children.text: vipravrājinī vividhaṃ prakarṣeṇa vrajatīti vipravrājinī svairiṇītyarthaḥ
children.translated_text: The word <s>vipravrājinī</s> means one who wanders in various ways and excessively; the meaning is "a wanton woman."
"Not previously belonging to another" means one who has not been taken by another man, whether by gift or by enjoyment.
By this, a remarried woman is excluded.
For this very reason <s>Kāśyapa</s> says:
Seven kinds of maidens who have become remarriageable, the lowest of families, are to be avoided:
one given by speech, one given in the mind, one for whom the auspicious wedding rites have been performed,

children.text: udakasparśitā yā ca yā ca pāṇigṛhītikā
children.translated_text: one touched with water, one whose hand has been taken,

children.text: agniṃ parigatā yā ca punarbhūprasavā ca yā ||
children.translated_text: one who has gone around the fire, and one born of a remarried woman.
These, said by <s>Kāśyapa</s>, burn up the family like fire.
Thus.
<s>Baudhāyana</s> says:

children.text: vāgdattā manodattāgniṃ parigatā saptamaṃ padaṃ nītā bhuktā gṛhītagarbhā prasūtā ceti saptavidhā punarbhūḥ tāṃ gṛhītvā na prajāṃ na dharmaṃ vindet ||
children.translated_text: A remarriageable woman is of seven kinds: one promised by speech, one given in the mind, one who has gone around the fire, one led to the seventh step, one enjoyed, one who has conceived, and one who has given birth. Having taken her, a man obtains neither offspring nor dharma.
Thus.
<s>Nārada</s> also says:
She who is still a maiden, whose womb is uninjured, yet is tainted by the taking of the hand,
is declared the first kind of remarriageable woman when the rite of consecration is performed again.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> also says:

children.text: akṣatā ca kṣatā caiva punarbhūḥ saṃskṛtā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whether uninjured or injured, a woman consecrated again is a remarriageable woman.
Thus.
"Beloved" means lovely, one who brings delight to the mind and eyes of the man who is to marry her.
For this very reason <s>Āpastamba</s> says:
Prosperity lies with the woman on whom the mind and eyes are firmly fixed.
Thus.
"A non-sapiṇḍa" is now explained.

children.text: samāna ekaḥ piṇḍo yasyāḥ sā sapiṇḍā ||
children.translated_text: She for whom there is one and the same piṇḍa is <s>sapiṇḍā</s>.
One who is not sapiṇḍā is <s>asapiṇḍā</s>; her he should marry.
And sapiṇḍa-relationship extends up to the seventh person.
In that matter there is one giver of the piṇḍa, and three sharers in the piṇḍa: father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
Three are sharers in the lepa, beginning with the aged great-grandfather.
Accordingly, in the <s>Matsyapurāṇa</s>:
The sharers in the lepa are those beginning with the fourth; the father and the others are sharers in the piṇḍa.
The seventh among them is the giver of the piṇḍa; sapiṇḍa-relationship is seven-generational.
Thus.
<s>Mārkaṇḍeya</s> also says:
Father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather
are to be known as the three persons connected by the piṇḍa.
The others connected by the lepa are said to be three, beginning from the grandfather's grandfather;
and the sacrificer is the seventh among them.
This seven-generational relationship has been declared by the sages.
Thus.
This is what is meant: the participation of seven persons in one piṇḍa-rite is the cause of sapiṇḍa-relationship.

children.text: tathā ca devadattasya svakīyaiḥ pitrādibhiḥ ṣaḍbhiḥ saha sāpiṇḍyam ||
children.translated_text: Thus <s>Devadatta</s> has sapiṇḍa-relationship with his own six ancestors beginning with his father.

children.text: tathā putrādibhiḥ ṣaḍbhiḥ saha sāpiṇḍyam iti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise he has sapiṇḍa-relationship with his six descendants beginning with his son.

children.text: nanu evaṃ sati bhrātṛpitṛvyādibhiḥ saha sāpiṇḍyaṃ na syāt ||
children.translated_text: Objection: if this is so, there would be no sapiṇḍa-relationship with brothers, paternal uncles, and the like.
For they are not included among those enumerated.
Not so.
For what is intended here is unity of rite through unity of the deities to whom it is directed.

children.text: devadattakartṛkakriyāyāṃ ye devatātvenānupraviśanti teṣāṃ madhye yaḥ ko'pi bhrātṛpitṛvyakartṛkakriyāyām apyanupraviśatītyasti taiḥ saha sāpiṇḍyam ||
children.translated_text: Among those who enter as deities in the rite performed by <s>Devadatta</s>, any one person also enters in the rite performed by a brother or paternal uncle; therefore there is sapiṇḍa-relationship with them.
In the same way, wives too have sapiṇḍa-relationship because they are co-agents in the piṇḍa-offering rite performed by the husband.
This is sapiṇḍa-relationship based on the offering.
Others, however, explain sapiṇḍa-relationship differently.

children.text: tathā hi samāna ekaḥ piṇḍo dehāvayavau yeṣāṃ te sapiṇḍāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus: those whose bodily parts are one and the same piṇḍa are sapiṇḍas.

children.text: tatra putrasya sākṣāt pitṛdehāvayavānvayena pitrā saha sāpiṇḍyam ||
children.translated_text: In that view, a son has sapiṇḍa-relationship with his father because he directly descends from the bodily parts of the father.
Likewise he has it with the grandfather and others, through the father, because of descent from their bodily parts.
He has it with the mother because he directly descends from the bodily parts of the mother.
He has it with the maternal grandfather and others also, through the mother, because of descent from their bodily parts.
Likewise he has it with the paternal uncle, paternal aunt, and others because of descent from the bodily parts of the grandfather.
And with the maternal aunt, maternal uncle, and others because of descent from the body of the maternal grandfather.
The husband has sapiṇḍa-relationship with his wife because she is the originator of one body together with him.
So too the wives of brothers have it with their respective husbands, who are originators of one body, because of sharing in the origination of one body.

children.text: evaṃ tatra tatra sākṣāt paramparayā vā ekaśarīrāvayavānvayena sāpiṇḍyaṃ yojanīyam ||
children.translated_text: Thus in each case sapiṇḍa-relationship should be applied through descent from the parts of one body, either directly or through a chain.

children.text: uktaṃ dvividhaṃ sāpiṇḍyaṃ yasyā nāsti seyamasapiṇḍā tāmudvahet ||
children.translated_text: A man should marry that woman who lacks the two kinds of sapiṇḍa-relationship just described, for she is non-sapiṇḍa.

children.text: nanu evaṃ sati na kvāpyudvāhaḥ sambhavet ||
children.translated_text: Objection: if this is so, marriage could not occur anywhere.
For sapiṇḍa-relationship can somehow be applied everywhere.
Since continuity from the body of the creator is hard to avoid.
"May I become many; may I be born forth,"
so says scripture.
This is not a fault.

children.text: aviśeṣeṇa prāptasya sāpiṇḍyasya saptasu pañcasu ca puruṣeṣu saṃkucitatvena tadūrdhvaṃ sāpiṇḍyanivṛtteḥ ||
children.translated_text: For sapiṇḍa-relationship, though obtained without distinction, is restricted to seven and five generations, and beyond that sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases.
Accordingly <s>Gautama</s> says:
The cessation of piṇḍa-relationship is at the seventh or the fifth generation.
Thus.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> also says:
Beyond the fifth from the mother’s side and likewise beyond the seventh from the father’s side.
Thus.

children.text: mātṛpakṣe pañcamāt pitṛpakṣe saptamāt puruṣād ūrdhvaṃ sāpiṇḍyaṃ nivartate ityadhyāhṛtya yojanīyam ||
children.translated_text: This should be construed by supplying: on the mother’s side sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases beyond the fifth person, and on the father’s side beyond the seventh person.
But sapiṇḍa-status ceases in the seventh person.
Because of this recollection of <s>Manu</s>.
This is what is meant:

children.text: pitṛpakṣe kūṭastham ārabhya tatputrādigaṇanāyāṃ saptamād ūrdhvaṃ varavadhvor vivāho na duṣyati ||
children.translated_text: On the father’s side, beginning with the fixed ancestor and counting his son and the rest, beyond the seventh, the marriage of bridegroom and bride is not defective.

children.text: mātṛpakṣe ca kūṭasthamārabhya tatputrādiparigaṇanāyāṃ varavadhvor mātā cet pañcamī bhavati tadā tayoḥ sāpiṇḍyanivṛtter vivāho na doṣāyeti ||
children.translated_text: And on the mother’s side, beginning with the fixed ancestor and counting his son and the rest, if the mother of the bride and groom is the fifth, then, because their sapiṇḍa-relationship has ceased, the marriage is not blameworthy.
As for the statement of the <s>Viṣṇupurāṇa</s>:
A fifth woman from the mother’s side and a seventh from the father’s side,
a householder should marry as a wife, by the proper rule, O king.
Thus.
There one must supply: after passing beyond the seventh and the fifth.
Otherwise,
Beyond the fifth and beyond the seventh,
there would be contradiction with this statement.

children.text: pañcame saptame caiva yeṣāṃ vaivāhikī kriyā
children.translated_text: Those whose marriage rite is performed in the fifth and seventh generations,

children.text: kriyāparā api hi te sarvataḥ śūdratāṃ gatāḥ ||
children.translated_text: even though they are intent on rites, have in every way fallen into the condition of Śūdras.
And because it would contradict this statement of <s>Marīci</s>.
Although <s>Paiṭhīnasi</s> has stated two alternatives:
One should avoid the fifth from the mother and the seventh from the father,
or three from the mother and five from the father.
Thus.
There the second alternative concerns persons not of the same caste.
For <s>Śaṅkha</s> says:
If many are born of one caste, but from separate fields and with separate property,

children.text: ekapiṇḍāḥ pṛthakśaucāḥ piṇḍas tv āvartate triṣu ||
children.translated_text: they have one piṇḍa but separate impurity; the piṇḍa, however, recurs among three.
Thus.
This is the meaning:

children.text: yeṣāmekaḥ pitā mātaro bhinnajātīyās te mātṛbhedād asamānajātīyāḥ tathāpi pitraikyādasti teṣāṃ sāpiṇḍyam ||
children.translated_text: Those who have one father but mothers of different castes are, because of the difference of mothers, not of the same caste; nevertheless, because the father is one, sapiṇḍa-relationship exists for them.
And that ceases when three generations have passed.

children.text: nanu evaṃ sati pitṛpakṣe 'pi tribhiḥ puruṣaiḥ sāpiṇḍyanivṛtteḥ pañca pitṛto vā iti vacanaṃ virudhyeta ||
children.translated_text: Objection: if that is so, then on the father’s side too, since sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with three generations, the statement 'or five from the father' would be contradicted.
If so, then:
Three from the mother or five from the father,
this statement of <s>Paiṭhīnasi</s> is meant only as a prohibition within the nearer limit among persons of the same caste.
Or else let it be a secondary alternative.
In 'from the mother and likewise from the father,'
the word 'father' also includes the begetter.
And accordingly <s>Gautama</s> says:
Beyond the seventh from the paternal relatives,
and from the begetter,
and beyond the fifth from the maternal relatives.
Thus.

children.text: yo hi niyogāt putramutpādayati sa bījī ||
children.translated_text: For one who begets a son by niyoga is the begetter.
The paternal and maternal relatives are described in another smṛti:

children.text: pituḥ pitṛṣvasuḥ putrāḥ pitur mātṛṣvasuḥ sutāḥ
children.translated_text: The sons of the father’s paternal aunt, the sons of the father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of the father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal relatives.
The sons of the mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of the mother’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of the mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives.
Thus.
Objection: the phrase 'not a sapiṇḍa' need not be stated.
For the prohibition against marrying a sapiṇḍa is already established by the later phrase 'born in a different ārṣa gotra.'
True.

children.text: tathāpi yā māturasapiṇḍā bhavati saivodvāhakarmaṇi praśasteti vaktum ||
children.translated_text: Still, it is said in order to state that she who is not a sapiṇḍa of the mother is especially approved in the marriage rite.
And so <s>Manu</s> says:

children.text: asapiṇḍā ca yā māturasagotrā ca yā pituḥ
children.translated_text: She who is not a sapiṇḍa of the mother and who is not of the same gotra as the father,
she is approved for twice-born men in the wife-taking rite, for union.
Thus.

children.text: yā māturasapiṇḍā asagotrā ca yā piturasagotrā cakārādasapiṇḍā ca sā maithune mithunasādhye dārakarmaṇi dvijātīnāṃ praśastā pariṇeyetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: she who is not a sapiṇḍa of the mother, and she who is not of the same gotra as the father, and, by the word 'and,' is also not a sapiṇḍa of the father, is approved as one to be married by twice-born men in the wife-taking rite, which is accomplished through union.
Objection: here the mention of the mother is useless.
For by prohibiting the father’s gotra and sapiṇḍa-relationship, the prohibition of the mother’s gotra and sapiṇḍa-relationship is already established.
Because she has no separate piṇḍa or gotra.

children.text: ekatvaṃ sā gatā bhartuḥ piṇḍe gotre ca sūtake
children.translated_text: She has gone into unity with her husband in piṇḍa, gotra, and impurity;
a woman falls away from her own gotra at marriage, at the seventh step.
Because of this statement.
Not so.
For in gāndharva and other marriages, because there is no giving of the maiden, the father’s gotra and sapiṇḍa-relationship do not cease.
And accordingly the <s>Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa</s> says:

children.text: brāhmādiṣu vivāheṣu yā tūḍhā kanyakā bhavet
children.translated_text: A maiden who has been married in the brāhma and other forms of marriage,
for her the piṇḍa-and-water rite should be performed according to the husband’s gotra.
In gāndharva and other marriages it is according to the father’s gotra, in accordance with dharma.
Thus.
By this, the dispute concerning marriage with a maternal uncle’s daughter is also refuted.
For the prohibitory statements on that matter concern one born from a woman married by a gāndharva or similar form of marriage.
Because in that case sapiṇḍa-relationship has not ceased.
They do not concern one born from a woman married by the brāhma and other forms, because scripture, smṛti, and good custom support that case.
For there sapiṇḍa-relationship has ceased.
And those prohibitory statements are as follows.
There <s>Śātātapa</s> says:
Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, and likewise a woman of the mother’s gotra,
or one with the same pravara, a twice-born man should perform a cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus.
<s>Paiṭhīnasi</s> also says:
The daughters of the father’s and mother’s sisters, and daughters of the maternal uncle, are by dharma sisters.
It is understood that he should avoid them.
Thus.
<s>Sumantu</s> also says:
All the wives of the father are mothers;
their brothers are maternal uncles;
their sisters are maternal aunts;
and their daughters are sisters;
their children are nephews and nieces,
otherwise they cause mixture of lineage.
Thus.
<s>Vyāsa</s>:
The <s>sapiṇḍa</s> relatives of the mother are to be carefully avoided by twice-born men.
Thus.

children.text: nanu aviśeṣeṇa pravṛttānāmeṣāṃ vacanānāṃ kathaṃ viśeṣaviṣayatā viśeṣavacanabalāditi brūmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Objection: since these statements operate without distinction, how can they be said to concern a specific subject? We reply: by the force of a statement of specification.
And so <s>Manu</s> says:
Having approached the daughter of his father's sister, his sister, the daughter of his own sister, or of his mother,

children.text: mātuśca bhrātur āptasya gatvā cāndrāyaṇaṃ caret ||
children.translated_text: or the daughter of the mother's near brother, he should perform the cāndrāyaṇa penance.
But a wise man should not take these three as wives.
Thus.
The word "sister" qualifies such terms as "daughter of the father's sister."
"Near" qualifies "mother's brother."
There the word "daughter" is to be supplied.

children.text: āptasya saṃnikṛṣṭasya sapiṇḍasya gāndharvādivivāhoḍhāyāḥ māturbhrātur ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is: of the mother's brother who is near, close, and <s>sapiṇḍa</s>, born from a mother married by a gāndharva or similar marriage.
In the expression "daughter of the father's sister" too, the intended sense is a father's sister whose <s>sapiṇḍa</s> relation has not ceased and who was married by a gāndharva or similar marriage.

children.text: tathā ca sati tadduhitur bhaginīti viśeṣaṇaṃ sārthakam ||
children.translated_text: And when that is so, the qualifier "sister" for her daughter is meaningful.
In brāhma and similar marriages, because the <s>sapiṇḍa</s> relation ceases, the word "sister" would not apply.

children.text: ayam eva nyāyo mātṛṣvasrīyāyām api yojanīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This same principle should also be applied to the daughter of the mother's sister.

children.text: tasmād bhaginyāptapadopetamanuvacanabalād aviśeṣe niṣedho viśeṣaviṣaya evopasaṃhriyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, by the force of <s>Manu</s>'s statement furnished with the words "sister" and "near," the prohibition, though general, is restricted to a specific subject.

children.text: nanu brāhmādivivāhaviṣaye mātulasutāyā iva mātṛṣvasṛsutāyā api vivāhaḥ prāpnuyāt ||
children.translated_text: Objection: in the case of brāhma and similar marriages, marriage with the daughter of the mother's sister would also follow, just as with the daughter of the maternal uncle.
That is not so.
Because, since it is censured by respectable people, one must infer a prohibitive smṛti there.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> states that what is censured by respectable people is not to be adopted:
One should not practice even a dharma that does not lead to heaven and is hated by the world.
Thus.

children.text: yadyapi mātulasutāpariṇayanam udīcyaśiṣṭagarhitaṃ tathāpi dākṣiṇātyaśiṣṭair ācaritatvena nāvigīto 'yam udīcyānāmācāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although the marrying of a maternal uncle's daughter is censured by respectable northerners, still, because it is practiced by respectable southerners, this custom of the northerners is not without opposition.
Nor should it be suspected that the southerners act from passion as their basis.
For that marriage is performed precisely by those who examine injunctions and prohibitions.
But marriage with the daughter of the mother's sister is censured by an uncontested practice of respectable people.
Vedic texts and the like support marriage with a maternal uncle's daughter.
There the mantra-text is:

children.text: āyāhīndra pathibhir īḍitebhir yajñamimaṃ no bhāgadheyaṃ juṣasva
children.translated_text: Come, O <s>Indra</s>, by the praised paths; enjoy this sacrifice of ours, your allotted share.

children.text: tṛptāṃ jahurmātulasyeva yoṣā bhāgaste paitṛṣvaseyī vapām iva ||
children.translated_text: They have abandoned the satisfied woman of the maternal uncle, as it were; your share is the daughter of the father's sister, as it were, the omentum.
Thus.

children.text: ayamarthaḥ he indra pathibhir īḍitebhiḥ stutaiḥ saha no 'smākamimaṃ yajñamāyāhi ||
children.translated_text: This is the meaning: O <s>Indra</s>, come to this sacrifice of ours together with the praised, lauded paths.

children.text: āgatya ca asmādibhir dīyamānaṃ bhāgadheyaṃ juṣasva ||
children.translated_text: And having come, enjoy the allotted share being given by us.

children.text: tṛptām ājyādinā saṃskṛtāṃ vapāṃ tvāmuddiśya jahuḥ tyaktavantaḥ ||
children.translated_text: They have offered, for your sake, the omentum that has been prepared with ghee and the like, as one that is satisfied.
There are two comparisons for you.

children.text: yathā mātulasya yoṣā duhitā bhāgineyasya bhāgaḥ bhajanīyā bhāgineyena pariṇetuṃ yogyā yathā ca paitṛṣvaseyī pautrasya bhāgaḥ tathāyaṃ te tava bhāgo vapākhyaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: Just as the maternal uncle's woman, that is, his daughter, is the share of the sister's son, to be enjoyed and fit to be married by the sister's son, and just as the daughter of the father's sister is the grandson's share, so this share of yours is the one called the omentum.
Also in the <s>Vājasaneyaka</s>:

children.text: tasmādvā samānādeva puruṣādattā cādyaśca jāyate uta tṛtīye saṃgacchāvahai caturthe saṃgacchāvahai ||
children.translated_text: Therefore from the very same man are born both the eater and what is to be eaten; let us come together in the third generation, let us come together in the fourth.
Thus.

children.text: samānādekasmāt puruṣād attā bhoktā adyaśca bhogyaḥ dvāvapyutpadyete ||
children.translated_text: From the same single man both are produced: the eater, that is, the enjoyer, and what is to be eaten, that is, the object of enjoyment.

children.text: tau ca mithaḥ saṃkalpayataḥ kūṭasthamārabhya tṛtīye caturthe vā puruṣe saṃgacchāvahai vivahāvahai ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the two form the mutual resolve: beginning from the common ancestor, let us come together in the third or fourth person, that is, let us marry.

children.text: yadyapyayam arthavādaḥ tathāpi mānāntaravirodhābhāvāt svārthe pramāṇam ||
children.translated_text: Although this is an arthavāda, still, because there is no contradiction from another means of knowledge, it is authoritative in its own meaning.
For there are no opposing statements.
And because it has been explained that the rule does not concern the mother's <s>sapiṇḍa</s> relatives.

children.text: tasmād aviruddhārthavādenānūditatvād uparidhāraṇavad vidhiḥ kalpayituṃ śakyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because it is restated by a non-contradictory arthavāda, an injunction can be inferred, as in the case of holding above.
Thus it is heard in the funerary agnihotra:

children.text: adhastāt samidhaṃ dhārayannanudravet upari hi devebhyo yajñaṃ dhārayati
children.translated_text: He should run after it holding the fuel-stick below, for he holds the sacrifice above for the gods.
Thus.

children.text: tatra paitṛkasya haviṣo 'dhastāt samantrakaṃ samiddhāraṇaṃ vidhāya tadvākyaśeṣeṇa samidho haviruparidhāraṇaṃ daive karmaṇi yat śrutaṃ tat kimarthavādaḥ uta vidhirayam iti saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, after enjoining the holding of the fuel-stick with mantra below the ancestral oblation, the remainder of that sentence mentions holding the fuel-stick above the oblation in a divine rite. The doubt is whether this is an arthavāda or an injunction.

children.text: tatrādhodhāraṇavidhistāvakatvena tadekavākyatālābhād arthavāda iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: On this point, the prima facie view is that, since it has unity of sentence as praising the injunction to hold below, it is an arthavāda.
For it is proper that praise should be made by restating a well-known matter.

children.text: upari dhāraṇaṃ tu na kvāpi prasiddham ||
children.translated_text: But holding above is not established anywhere.

children.text: atastāvakatvāyogād vākyabhedam abhyupagamyāpy apūrvārthatvād vidhiḥ kalpitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because it cannot serve as praise and because it has a new meaning, even while accepting a division of the sentence, it is inferred to be an injunction.

children.text: evaṃ tṛtīye puruṣe saṃgacchāvahai ityādāvapi apūrvārthatvena mātulasutāṃ vivahed iti vidhiḥ kalpyate ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, in passages such as "let us come together in the third generation," because they have a new meaning, an injunction is inferred: one should marry the maternal uncle's daughter.
Therefore this marriage is supported in śruti.
The smṛtis too have been shown to lead to marriage with the maternal uncle's daughter by removing <s>sapiṇḍa</s> relation in brāhma and similar marriages.
And the uncontested practice of respectable southerners has been cited.

children.text: kecittu āsurādiṣvapi deśaviśeṣeṇa mātulasutāvivāho dharmya iti manyante ||
children.translated_text: Some, however, think that even among āsura and similar marriages, according to particular regions, marriage with the maternal uncle's daughter is dharmic.
And they cite statements.
There <s>Baudhāyana</s> says:
In the south there is fivefold disagreement:

children.text: anupanītena bhāryayā ca sahabhojanaṃ paryuṣitabhojanaṃ mātuladuhitṛpitṛṣvasṛduhitṛpariṇayanam iti
children.translated_text: eating together with an uninitiated man and with one's wife, eating stale food, and marrying the daughter of the maternal uncle and the daughter of the father's sister.

children.text: tathottarata ūrṇāvikrayaḥ sīdhupānam ubhayato'dadbhir vyavahāraḥ āyudhīyakaṃ samudrayānam iti
children.translated_text: Likewise, in the northern region there are the sale of wool, drinking liquor, dealings with those who do not give on either side, military service, and sea-voyage, and so on.
One who performs the practice of the other in the other's region becomes blameworthy, one in the other's region.
In each such case, the authority of the region itself should hold.
Thus.

children.text: itaro dākṣiṇātya itarasmin uttaradeśe mātulasambandhaṃ kurvan duṣyati ||
children.translated_text: The other, a southerner, becomes blameworthy when in the northern country he makes a maternal-uncle connection.
Not in his own region.

children.text: tathetara udīcya itarasmin dakṣiṇadeśe sīdhupānādikaṃ kurvan duṣyati ||
children.translated_text: Likewise the other, a northerner, becomes blameworthy when in the southern country he drinks liquor and the like.
Not in his own region.
Why? Because of the authority of regional usage.
The meaning is: because the authority of custom is dependent on region.
And accordingly <s>Devala</s> says:

children.text: yasmin deśe ya ācāro nyāyadṛṣṭaḥ sukalpitaḥ
children.translated_text: Whatever custom in a given region is seen as just and well established,

children.text: sa tasminneva kartavyo na tu deśāntare smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that alone is to be performed in that region, but it is not prescribed in another region.
Thus.
<s>Bhṛgu</s> says:

children.text: yasmin deśe pure grāme naividye nagare 'pi vā
children.translated_text: In whatever country, town, village, settlement, or even city,

children.text: yo yatra vihito dharmastaṃ dharmaṃ na vicālayet ||
children.translated_text: whatever <s>dharma</s> has been enjoined there, one should not disturb that <s>dharma</s>.
Thus.
Objection: if the conduct of the learned has authority, then marriage with one's own daughter too would follow.
Because <s>Prajāpati</s> acted in that way.
And so scripture says:
<s>Prajāpati</s>, indeed, desired his own daughter.
Thus.
Not so.
Because of the maxim, 'one should not practice the conduct of the gods.'
For this very reason <s>Baudhāyana</s> says:

children.text: anuṣṭhitaṃ tu yaddevair munibhir yad anuṣṭhitam
children.translated_text: What has been practiced by the gods, and what has been practiced by the sages,
is not to be practiced by human beings; one should perform the act that is prescribed.
Thus.

children.text: tadevaṃ pūrvoktabrāhmādivivāhavyavasthayā deśabhedaviṣayavyavasthayā ca mātulasutāvivāhaḥ sapiṇḍām ityādiśāstrādeva siddhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in this way, by the previously stated rule concerning the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, and by the rule concerning distinctions of region, marriage with a maternal uncle's daughter is established precisely from scriptural statements such as 'a <s>sapiṇḍā</s>,' and so forth.
'Younger' means deficient in age and also in bodily size.
On this point <s>Manu</s> states the measure of being deficient in age:
A man of twenty years should marry a pleasing girl of twelve years,
or a man of twenty-four years an eight-year-old girl, if he is quickly sinking with regard to <s>dharma</s>.
Thus.
<s>Bṛhaspati</s> also says:

children.text: triṃśadvarṣo daśābdāṃ tu bhāryāṃ vindeta nagnikām
children.translated_text: A man of thirty years should take as wife a ten-year-old girl who is not yet menstruating,
or a man of twenty-one years may obtain a seven-year-old girl.
Thus.
Also in the <s>Viṣṇupurāṇa</s>:
Being himself three times her age, he should marry a wife of one-third his years.
Thus.
'Healthy' means free from incurable diseases such as pulmonary consumption and the like.

children.text: bhrātṛmatīṃ jyeṣṭhaḥ kaniṣṭho vā bhrātā yasyāḥ sā bhrātṛmatī ||
children.translated_text: 'Having a brother' means: she who has an elder or younger brother is <s>bhrātṛmatī</s>, one having a brother.
By this, suspicion that she is a <s>putrikā</s> (appointed daughter) is removed.
For this very reason <s>Manu</s> says:

children.text: yasyāstu na bhaved bhrātā na vijñāyeta vā pitā
children.translated_text: But she who has no brother, or whose father is not known,
the wise man should not marry her, because of suspicion regarding the law of an appointed daughter.
Thus.

children.text: yasyāḥ pitā putrikākaraṇābhiprāyavān vā na vā iti na vijñāyate tāṃ nopayacchet ||
children.translated_text: He should not marry her of whom it is not known whether her father has the intention of making her an appointed daughter or not.
